title: Hearing: how two ears find where a sound is, and why noise can hide a voice

summary.text: Sit with your eyes shut while someone clinks a spoon on a katori somewhere around you. You can point straight at it. Now cover one ear and point again, and your finger goes wrong. The sound has not changed. Each ear only picks up how loud the sound is and the moment it arrives, and your brain works out the place from the difference between the two ears. Your child tests this, then finds out why a running tap can hide a whisper that is still reaching her ears, how the decibel scale grows, and how the inner ear sorts high notes from low ones along a coiled tube no longer than a thumb. The unit goes on to hearing aids, cochlear implants and sign language, and to the ears on a cricket's front legs. A Hungarian scientist, Georg von Békésy, showed in the 1940s that the ear sorts pitches with a travelling wave, and not with strings as the German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz had guessed.
summary.art: A girl sitting blindfolded in the middle of a room pointing at a spoon being clinked on a steel katori, with two faint curved lines from the katori reaching her two ears at slightly different lengths.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. A friend claps somewhere in the room. Without peeking, point to where the clap came from. Now cover one ear with a cap or your hand and try again. Which time do you point better, and why?
intro.text: With two ears open, you point well. With one ear covered, you miss by a lot. A sound is just a wave in the air, and it carries no label that says where it came from. Your brain works out the place by comparing what the two ears hear. In this unit you test that yourself. You also find out why a loud sound can hide a quiet one, how the inner ear sorts high and low notes, how hearing aids and signing help people who hear less, and how other animals hear with their knees, their antennae and their jaws.
intro.art: A child in the middle of a room with a scarf over her eyes, one ear covered by a cap, pointing in the wrong direction while a parent stands to her left holding a steel katori and spoon.

outcomes: I can explain how two ears tell where a sound is, using the tiny differences in time and loudness between them.
I can test how well I find where a sound is with two ears and with one ear covered, and explain what I find.
I can read a decibel number, say how the scale grows, and use it to judge how long a sound is safe to listen to.
I can explain why a loud sound can hide a quiet one, and what a speaker can do to be heard in noise.
I can describe how the cochlea sorts high and low pitches along its length, and how hair cells send signals to the brain.
I can say how hearing aids and cochlear implants help, and how people who cannot hear communicate and enjoy music.
I can tell how Georg von Békésy found a travelling wave in the ear, and give examples of ears in unusual places.

terms.meaning: Where a sound comes from. Scientists call finding it sound localisation.
terms.example: When a cuckoo calls in a tree, you turn your head to the right tree without thinking. That is your sense of sound direction.
terms.art: A child turning her head towards a bird calling from a tree on her right.

terms.meaning: The tiny gap between the moment a sound reaches the nearer ear and the moment it reaches the farther ear.
terms.example: A clap on your right reaches your right ear about six ten-thousandths of a second before your left ear. That is much too short to notice, yet your brain uses it.
terms.art: A head seen from above with a clap on the right, and two arrows of different lengths to the right ear and the left ear.

terms.meaning: The way your head blocks some sound from reaching the far ear, so the far ear hears it a little softer.
terms.example: A whistle on your left sounds a little softer in your right ear, because your head is in the way.
terms.art: A head seen from above with a whistle on the left, and a soft area behind the head on the right.

terms.meaning: The part of the ear you can see on the side of your head, the ear flap. Its folds change sounds a little depending on the direction they come from.
terms.example: Folded forwards, your pinna lets in more sound from the front. Cupped behind with a hand, it catches more sound from the back.
terms.art: A side view of an ear with its folds and an arrow from the front and an arrow from behind.

terms.meaning: The unit for how strong a sound is. The short way to write it is dB. Zero decibels is about the faintest sound a young person can hear.
terms.example: A whisper is about 30 decibels. A normal conversation is about 60. A motorbike passing close is about 95.
terms.art: A ladder with a whisper at the bottom, a conversation in the middle and a motorbike near the top, each with its decibel number.

terms.meaning: When a loud sound hides a quieter one, so that you cannot hear the quiet one even though it is still reaching your ear.
terms.example: You cannot hear a friend whisper while the water tap is running hard.
terms.art: A girl listening to a whisper while a tap runs, with the whisper wave drawn small and the tap noise drawn large over it.

terms.meaning: Your ability to pick out one voice in a noisy crowd by listening only to it. It was named after a party, but it happens in any crowd.
terms.example: At a wedding hall full of talk, you can still follow your cousin's voice, and you notice if someone across the hall says your name.
terms.art: A girl in a crowded hall with many speech bubbles around her and one bubble linked to her ear by a thick line.

terms.meaning: A thin strip inside the cochlea that moves when sound arrives. It is stiff and narrow at the start of the cochlea and soft and wide at the far end.
terms.example: Unrolled, the basilar membrane is about as long as the width of your thumb.
terms.art: A long thin strip that is narrow at one end and wide at the other, with hair cells drawn along it.

terms.meaning: A wave that moves along the basilar membrane when sound arrives. It grows to a peak at one place and then dies away. The place of the peak depends on the pitch.
terms.example: A high note makes the wave peak near the start of the cochlea. A low note makes it peak near the far end.
terms.art: A strip with two waves on it: one peaking near the narrow end and another peaking near the wide end.

terms.meaning: About 12,000 tiny cells in each cochlea that make the wave on the basilar membrane bigger and sharper, so that we can hear very quiet sounds.
terms.example: When loud noise damages the outer hair cells, quiet sounds become hard to hear, and sounds that are close in pitch become hard to tell apart.
terms.art: Rows of tiny hair cells on a strip, with small arrows showing them pushing up on the strip.

terms.meaning: The quietest sound a person can just hear. It is different for each pitch.
terms.example: You find your threshold at a pitch by turning a sound down until you can only just hear it.
terms.art: A curve on a graph with a person at one end turning a volume dial down.

terms.meaning: A chart of a person's hearing threshold at different pitches. Each ear has its own line.
terms.example: An audiogram of a child with normal hearing is a line near the top of the chart. A line that drops at the right end means high sounds are hard to hear.
terms.art: A chart with pitch along the bottom and loudness down the side, with two curved lines marked right ear and left ear.

terms.meaning: A small device worn in or behind the ear that makes sounds louder, using a microphone, an amplifier and a tiny speaker.
terms.example: A grandfather who hears speech faintly can wear a hearing aid that makes the voices louder.
terms.art: A small hearing aid behind an ear with a tiny tube going into the ear canal.

terms.meaning: A device that is placed in the ear by an operation. It sends signals from a microphone straight to the hearing nerve through about twenty tiny wires, instead of using the hair cells.
terms.example: A child who was born with no working hair cells can hear speech with a cochlear implant.
terms.art: A cutaway of an ear showing a thin wire coiled inside the cochlea and a small round piece behind the ear.

terms.meaning: A full language of hand shapes, movements and faces, used by Deaf people across India. It has its own words and its own grammar, different from spoken Hindi or English.
terms.example: Two Deaf friends can chat for an hour in Indian Sign Language without any sound.
terms.art: Two people facing each other, signing with their hands near their faces.

terms.meaning: A ringing, buzzing or hissing that a person hears when there is no sound outside.
terms.example: After a very loud concert, many people hear a ringing in their ears for a few hours.
terms.art: A person with a hand on her ear and small ringing lines near her head.

terms.meaning: Three small fluid-filled loops in the inner ear, one for each way the head can turn. They tell the brain when your head moves.
terms.example: When you spin around and stop, the fluid keeps moving for a moment, and the world seems to spin.
terms.art: An inner ear with three loops at right angles and a snail-shaped cochlea beside them.

terms.meaning: Tiny stones made of chalk that sit on hair cells in the ears of fish and in the balance part of our ears. They help sense sound, gravity and movement.
terms.example: A rohu fish has ear stones inside her head and she can tell which way is down.
terms.art: A fish with a magnified cutaway showing a small white stone sitting on a bed of hair cells inside her head.

explanations.concept: Two ears tell where a sound is
explanations.context: This card explains how two ears find the direction of a sound, which you test in the Sound Clock.
explanations.definition: A sound from one side reaches the nearer ear a tiny moment earlier and a little louder. The brain compares the two ears and works out the direction.
explanations.description: Your ears are about 20 centimetres apart. Sound in air travels about 340 metres each second. So a clap right beside your right ear needs about six ten-thousandths of a second longer to reach your left ear. You do not notice that moment. But the brain can notice a difference as small as about one hundred-thousandth of a second, which tells it the direction to within a few degrees. Your head also blocks some sound, so the far ear hears a high sound a little softer. The brain combines the two clues. For low sounds the timing clue works best. For high sounds the loudness clue works best. A sound straight in front or straight behind reaches both ears together and equally loudly, so these two places are easy to mix up. With one ear covered, both clues vanish, and the brain has to guess.
examples: A clap on your right reaches your right ear first and is a little louder there.
A sound straight ahead reaches both ears at the same time and equally loudly.
With one ear blocked, you tend to point towards the open ear, because the sound seems louder there.
explanations.art: A head seen from above, a clap on the right, a short wave line to the right ear and a longer wave line to the left ear with the head shadow shown.

explanations.concept: The ear flap, head turns and the front-back puzzle
explanations.context: This card says why sounds from the front and the back can be mixed up, and how to solve it.
explanations.definition: The folds of the pinna change a sound a little depending on its direction, and turning the head changes what each ear hears. Both help the brain tell front from back and up from down.
explanations.description: A sound straight in front and a sound straight behind reach both ears at the same time. So time and loudness do not tell them apart. The folds of the pinna help, because sound from the front is shaped in a slightly different way from sound from behind. The brain learns these shapes over many years. In experiments, people who wore small moulds that changed the folds of their pinnae were at first confused about up and down, and then learned again over some weeks. The easiest fix is to turn your head. Turn your head to the left. Now a sound in front is closer to your right ear, and a sound behind is closer to your left ear. Animals do this all the time. A cat swivels her ears to listen. Dogs and horses turn their pinnae separately. A barn owl has ears at different heights, so she can tell whether a mouse is above or below her.
examples: A sound straight ahead moves to your right ear when you turn your head to the left.
A cat turns her ears towards a noise to hear the noise better.
A barn owl has one ear opening higher than the other, so she can tell up from down.
explanations.art: A head seen from above turning left with a source in front moving to the right ear and a source behind moving to the left ear.

explanations.context: This card says how to read a decibel number and why the numbers grow in a special way.
explanations.definition: The decibel scale measures how strong a sound is. Every 10 decibels more means 10 times as much sound energy, and a sound that seems about twice as loud.
explanations.description: A whisper is about 30 decibels. A conversation is about 60. That is 30 decibels more, which is three steps of 10. Each step multiplies the sound energy by 10, so a conversation has 10 times 10 times 10, or 1,000 times, the energy of a whisper. Yet it only sounds about 8 times as loud to us, because our ears squash a very big range into a smaller one. That is why the scale is useful. Our ears can handle sounds from the faintest we can hear to a jet plane close by. The jet has about ten trillion times as much energy as the faintest sound, yet the decibel numbers only go from 0 to about 130. Common sounds: leaves rustling about 20, a quiet room 35, a refrigerator 40, a busy street 80, a mixer-grinder 85 to 90, a motorbike passing close 95, a car horn close by 110, a firecracker close by 140.
examples: A conversation at 60 decibels has 1,000 times the sound energy of a whisper at 30 decibels.
A busy street at 80 decibels sounds about 4 times as loud as a conversation at 60.
Sounds above 120 decibels can hurt at once, because they are far above the loudest comfortable level.
explanations.art: A tall ladder of sounds from leaves at the bottom to a firecracker at the top, with decibel numbers and arrows showing ten times steps.

explanations.concept: How long is a sound safe?
explanations.context: This card gives the rule for how long you can listen to a loud sound without harming your ears.
explanations.definition: The louder a sound, the shorter the time it is safe to listen. Health agencies say that about 85 decibels is safe for about 8 hours, and that every 3 decibels more means half the safe time.
explanations.description: The hair cells in your cochlea can be damaged by loud sound, and in people they do not grow back. Damage depends on both the loudness and the time. At 85 decibels, such as a mixer-grinder or very heavy traffic, the safe time is about 8 hours. At 88 decibels it is about 4 hours. At 91 it is about 2 hours, at 94 about 1 hour, at 97 about 30 minutes and at 100 decibels about 15 minutes. At 110 decibels, such as a loudspeaker at a wedding, harm can start in a minute or two. Indian rules for noise say that in homes and residential areas, sound should be no more than 55 decibels by day and 45 by night, and that a firecracker should not be louder than about 125 decibels when measured 4 metres away. Wearing earplugs or moving away lowers the level a lot. Most hearing damage from noise causes no pain at the time, which is why we must go by the numbers. Never push cotton buds, pins or anything else into the ear. The ear cleans itself, and a push can hurt the eardrum.
examples: At 85 decibels, about 8 hours is the safe limit.
At 100 decibels, such as a drill or a motorbike near the ear, only about 15 minutes is safe.
Each extra 3 decibels halves the safe time, so 97 decibels gives half the time of 94.
explanations.art: A table of decibel levels with a shrinking clock beside each, 8 hours at 85, 4 hours at 88, 2 hours at 91 and 15 minutes at 100.

explanations.concept: Why a sound gets fainter as you move away
explanations.context: In Doubling the Distance, you measured the sound of a fan at four distances and saw it drop each time the distance doubled. This card explains why.
explanations.definition: Sound spreads out in every direction, so the same energy covers a bigger and bigger area as you move away. In open air, each time you double the distance, the sound level falls by about 6 decibels.
explanations.description: When a marble drops into water, the ring of ripples gets lower as it spreads, because its energy is shared along a longer ring. Sound in the air spreads over the surface of a growing ball. Doubling the distance makes the ball four times bigger in area, so each bit gets a quarter of the energy. A quarter of the energy is about 6 decibels less. So if a fan reads 60 decibels at 1 metre, it reads about 54 at 2 metres, 48 at 4 metres and 42 at 8 metres in the open. Inside a room, the walls bounce some sound back, so the drop is usually smaller, about 3 to 5 decibels for each doubling. This is why the first step away from a loudspeaker helps a lot, and why a whisper only reaches a few metres.
examples: A fan that reads 60 decibels at 1 metre reads about 54 decibels at 2 metres in the open.
Moving from 1 metre to 8 metres away from a loudspeaker lowers the level by about 18 decibels in the open.
A whisper that is clear at 1 metre can be lost at 5 metres, because it has spread out and is smaller than the noise of the room.
explanations.art: A speaker at the left with four rings spreading out, the rings drawn fainter as they get bigger, with the numbers 60, 54, 48 and 42 beside them.

explanations.concept: Masking: why noise hides a voice
explanations.context: In Hiding a Whisper, a running tap stopped you hearing a whisper. This card explains why, and how your brain picks out one voice.
explanations.definition: Masking happens when a louder sound makes a quieter sound impossible to hear, even though the quieter sound still reaches the ear. Sounds close in pitch to the noise are masked the most.
explanations.description: In the Hiding a Whisper test, the whisper was still reaching your ears when the tap was running, but you did not hear it. The tap's sound moves the same part of the basilar membrane as the whisper does. The whisper's wave is much smaller than the tap's wave there, so it is lost. A sound that is far from the noise in pitch is masked less. This is why a thin, high whistle is easier to pick out among loud drums. It also helps to be close, because each time you halve the distance the voice gets a lot louder. And it helps to watch the speaker's mouth, because seeing the lips helps the brain fill in what the ear misses. The brain can also choose what to listen to. In a crowded hall you can follow one voice and ignore the rest. This is called the cocktail party effect. It needs both ears, because the brain uses the direction of each voice to separate them.
examples: You cannot hear a whisper while the tap runs full, though the whisper is still there.
A thin whistle is easier to hear over drums than a low voice, since its pitch is far from the drums.
In a crowded hall you can follow one friend's voice by listening only to it.
explanations.art: A basilar membrane strip with a large bump from a tap noise and a small whisper bump hidden inside it.

explanations.concept: The cochlea sorts high and low pitches along its length
explanations.context: This card explains how the inner ear tells high notes from low notes.
explanations.definition: When sound enters the cochlea, it makes a wave travel along the basilar membrane. The wave peaks at a place that depends on the pitch. High pitches peak near the start. Low pitches peak near the far end.
explanations.description: The cochlea is a coiled tube about 3.5 centimetres long when unrolled, filled with fluid. Inside runs the basilar membrane. At the start it is narrow and stiff. At the far end it is about five times wider and much softer. A stiff, narrow part moves best for high sounds. A soft, wide part moves best for low sounds. So a sound of 10,000 hertz makes the wave peak near the start, and a sound of 100 hertz makes it peak near the far end. Along the membrane there are about 15,000 hair cells in each ear. Each hair cell sits at one place, so each one tells the brain about one pitch. About 30,000 nerve fibres carry the messages to the brain. The brain reads which hair cells are signalling, and so it knows the pitch. A sound with many pitches, such as a voice, makes many places move at once.
examples: A high whistle peaks near the start of the cochlea.
A low drum peaks near the far end of the cochlea.
A sound with many pitches, like a voice, makes many places on the membrane move at once.
explanations.art: An unrolled cochlea strip, narrow and stiff at one end and wide and soft at the other, with a high-pitch wave peaking near the narrow end and a low-pitch wave peaking near the wide end.

explanations.concept: Why the middle ear is needed: air to water
explanations.context: This card explains why sound goes through the eardrum and three tiny bones before it reaches the cochlea.
explanations.definition: Sound moving from air into a liquid mostly bounces back. The eardrum and three tiny bones collect the sound over a big area and push it into the cochlea's fluid over a small area, so that much more of the sound gets in.
explanations.description: If you call to a friend who is swimming underwater, almost all your voice bounces off the surface of the water and she can hardly hear you. Only about one-thousandth of the sound energy goes from air into water. Your cochlea is full of fluid, so it has the same problem. The middle ear is the answer. The eardrum is about twenty times bigger in area than the small window it pushes on, so the push is made much stronger. The three small bones also work as a lever. Together they let most of the sound in. The smallest of the three, the stirrup, is about 3 millimetres long. It is the smallest bone in the body. When the middle ear is blocked by a cold or fluid, sounds seem muffled because less sound gets through.
examples: A voice calling from above hardly reaches someone underwater, because most of the sound bounces off the surface.
A cold that blocks the middle ear makes everything seem muffled.
The stirrup, a bone about 3 millimetres long, is the smallest bone in the body.
explanations.art: A cutaway of the ear with a wide eardrum, three small bones and a small window, and an arrow showing a strong push into the fluid.

explanations.context: This card says that the ear is not just a microphone: it adds energy to the sound it hears.
explanations.definition: The outer hair cells push on the basilar membrane and make the wave bigger and sharper. This push is so strong that the ear itself gives off faint sounds, which doctors can record.
explanations.description: In 1978 a British scientist, David Kemp, found that a healthy ear, in a quiet room, can send out a tiny sound of its own. These sounds are called otoacoustic emissions. They come from the outer hair cells, which keep pushing the membrane at the pitch of the sound and so boost it. Without the boost, quiet sounds would be much harder to hear. Doctors now use a tiny microphone in the ear to record these emissions and check a newborn baby's hearing in a minute or two. The test does not need the baby to do anything. If the ear is healthy, the sound comes out. If the outer hair cells are damaged, it does not.
examples: A healthy ear sends out a faint sound that a tiny microphone can record.
Hospitals use this test to check a newborn baby's hearing, without the baby doing anything.
A damaged cochlea gives no emission, and so the test shows a problem.
explanations.art: A baby with a tiny earpiece in one ear connected to a screen showing a small wave line.

explanations.concept: When hearing is lost, and what can help
explanations.context: This card says why some people hear less, and how hearing aids and cochlear implants help.
explanations.definition: Hearing loss happens when sound cannot get through the outer or middle ear, or when the hair cells and nerve cannot send the signal on. Hearing aids make sound louder. Cochlear implants send signals straight to the nerve.
explanations.description: The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.5 billion people, about one in five, live with some hearing loss. Some loss comes from a blocked ear or fluid in the middle ear, which can often be treated. Other loss comes from hair cells damaged by loud noise, illness, some medicines or growing old. A hearing aid has a microphone, a small amplifier and a tiny speaker. It makes sound louder, so that the hair cells that still work get a bigger signal. If almost all the hair cells have been lost, a cochlear implant can help. A tiny microphone behind the ear sends signals to about twenty wires coiled inside the cochlea. Each wire sets off the nerve at its own place along the cochlea, so each wire stands for a different pitch, the way the cochlea itself sorts pitches. It sounds different from normal hearing, but many people, including children who were born deaf, learn to understand speech with it. Early tests and early help matter most for small children, who are learning to speak.
examples: A hearing aid makes sounds louder for a grandparent whose hair cells have worn out with age.
A cochlear implant can help a child who was born with no working hair cells.
A blocked ear from a cold can be treated, and hearing returns.
explanations.art: Three small pictures: an ear with wax blocking it, a hearing aid behind an ear, and a cochlear implant with its coil in a cochlea.

explanations.concept: Living without hearing: sign language and feeling music
explanations.context: This card is about the ways people who cannot hear communicate and enjoy music.
explanations.definition: Sign languages are full languages made of hand shapes, movements and facial expressions. Many Deaf people also feel music through their bodies.
explanations.description: A sign language is not a spoken language shown with the hands. Linguists have shown since the 1960s that sign languages have their own grammar and can say anything a spoken language can. India has its own, Indian Sign Language. The Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre in New Delhi, set up in 2015, works to make it widely used and taught. Deaf people also enjoy music. Evelyn Glennie, a Scottish percussionist, lost most of her hearing by about the age of twelve. She plays barefoot to feel the vibration of the floor and the drums through her feet, legs and hands, and she has played in concert halls all over the world. When you talk with someone who hears less, face them, keep your mouth visible, speak clearly without shouting, reduce background noise, and be patient.
examples: Indian Sign Language has its own words and grammar, and is not the same as spoken Hindi or English.
Evelyn Glennie plays percussion barefoot so that she can feel the vibrations of the music.
To talk with a person who hears less, face them and cut down the background noise.
explanations.art: A percussionist playing a drum barefoot on a stage with wavy lines rising from the floor to her feet and hands.

explanations.context: This card shows that not every animal hears with ears like ours.
explanations.definition: Other animals have ears of different shapes in different places. All of them turn a vibration into a signal for the animal's brain.
explanations.description: A grasshopper has her ears on the sides of her belly, each covered with a thin eardrum. A cricket or a katydid has her ears on her front legs, just below the knees. A male mosquito hears with his feathery antennae, and uses them to follow the wingbeat of a female, which is a sound of about 400 to 500 beats each second. A fish has no ear flap, but she has ear stones inside her head, and a line of sensors along her sides that feel water waves. A moth can hear a hunting bat and dive to escape. A barn owl has ear openings at different heights on her head, and she finds a mouse in total darkness. In every case a thin skin or a hair is moved by sound, and the movement is changed into signals. Ears were invented many times in the history of life.
examples: A cricket hears with ears below the knees on her front legs.
A male mosquito follows the wingbeat of a female with his antennae.
A moth hears a hunting bat's call and dives to escape.
explanations.art: A cricket with ears on her front legs, a grasshopper with an ear on her side, a mosquito with feathery antennae and an owl with ears at different heights, each with an arrow to the ear.

explanations.context: This card says what the other part of the inner ear does.
explanations.definition: Next to the cochlea, three fluid-filled loops and two small stone-covered patches sense movement of the head and which way is down. They are the balance part of the ear.
explanations.description: When your head turns, fluid in the loops lags behind a little and bends hair cells, just as sound bends the hair cells in the cochlea. The three loops are at right angles, so they can sense turns in every direction. The two patches have tiny stones on top of hair cells, and the stones are pulled by gravity, so they tell you which way is down and when you speed up or slow down. When you spin round and stop, the fluid keeps moving for a few moments and your brain thinks you are still spinning. That is dizziness. Balance also needs your eyes and the feel of your feet. When you close your eyes, you have to rely more on your ears and feet, which is why standing on one leg gets harder.
examples: After spinning around and stopping, the fluid in the loops keeps moving, so you feel dizzy.
Standing on one foot is harder with your eyes shut.
Tiny stones on hair cells tell you which way is down, even in the dark.
explanations.art: An inner ear with three loops at right angles and two small patches with tiny stones, with arrows for head turns.

explanations.concept: What is tinnitus, and where does it come from?
explanations.context: This card is about the ringing that some people hear when there is no sound outside, which scientists still argue about.
explanations.description: Many people hear a ringing, hissing or buzzing in a quiet room, with no sound outside. It often starts after loud noise or with hearing loss. Scientists agree that it is very common, but they do not agree on where it comes from. Some think it is made by damaged hair cells sending faulty signals. Others think the brain makes it, when it has less sound to listen to and turns up its own volume, so it begins to hear noise it makes itself.
examples: After a very loud concert, many people hear ringing for a few hours.
In a very quiet room, many people with healthy hearing notice a faint hiss.

perspectives.explanation: The ringing starts in the damaged ear, where faulty hair cells send false signals to the brain.
The ringing is made in the brain. When the ear sends less signal, the brain turns up its own volume, and then it hears its own noise.

explanations.art: A person lying in a quiet room with ringing lines near her head and a brain drawn above with a small dial.

explanations.concept: Is a sound in the air, or in the ear?
explanations.context: This card asks an old question: is a sound a wave in the air or something that happens when a listener hears it?
explanations.description: When a drum is struck, a wave moves through the air: the air is squeezed, then spread out, again and again. That is certain. But is that wave the sound, or is the sound what a listener hears? The first idea says a sound exists even with no one there. The second says a sound needs a listener. A wave has only an amount of energy and a number of squeezes each second. Loudness and pitch are what we hear when the wave reaches us. Each side is right about something. They disagree about what the word 'sound' should mean.
examples: A drum struck in an empty room makes a wave in the air.
Loudness and pitch are what a listener hears. The wave itself has a size, called its amplitude, and a number of squeezes each second, called its frequency.

perspectives.explanation: A sound is the pressure wave in the air. It exists whether anyone is there or not. Hearing is what an ear and brain do with it.
A sound is what a listener hears. A wave has only energy and a number of squeezes each second. Loudness, pitch and place are made by the ear and brain.

explanations.art: A drum in an empty forest with a wave in the air, and a girl with a hand to her ear listening to a wave arriving.

agreed.text: Animals with two ears use the tiny differences in time and loudness between the ears to find where a sound is.
agreed.evidence: People who have one ear blocked, or who are deaf in one ear, point to sounds badly. In experiments with headphones, delaying the sound in one ear by a tiny fraction of a second moves where the sound seems to be.

agreed.text: A loud sound can permanently damage the hair cells of the cochlea, and in people these cells do not grow back.
agreed.evidence: Hearing tests of workers in noisy factories show lasting loss. Looking at the cochlea under a microscope after loud noise shows missing hair cells.

agreed.text: Every 10 decibels more is 10 times the sound energy.
agreed.evidence: It follows from how the decibel scale is defined, and sound meters follow it.

agreed.text: A sound makes a travelling wave along the basilar membrane, and the place of its peak depends on the pitch.
agreed.evidence: Georg von Békésy saw it under a microscope in the 1940s. Later measurements in living animals confirmed it and showed that the outer hair cells sharpen the peak.

agreed.text: A loud sound can hide a quieter one that is close to it in pitch.
agreed.evidence: Hearing tests on thousands of people show that a quiet sound cannot be heard while a loud sound close to it in pitch is playing.

agreed.text: Sign languages are full languages with their own grammar.
agreed.evidence: Linguists have studied them since the 1960s. They have shown that children learn sign languages in the same stages as spoken languages, and that sign languages can say anything a spoken language can.

challenging.claim: We find where a sound is only from how loud it is in each ear.
challenging.for: A sound on your right is louder in your right ear, and that does help.
challenging.against: Experiments with headphones show that a tiny delay between the ears, with no change in loudness, also moves where a sound seems to be, especially for low sounds. The brain uses both clues.
challenging.context: This card is about whether loudness alone tells us the direction of a sound.

challenging.claim: Blind people sense walls and doors through the skin of their faces.
challenging.who: Many people in the 1800s and early 1900s, who called it facial vision
challenging.for: Blind people can walk along a corridor without touching walls, and some say they feel the wall on their face.
challenging.against: In 1944 Supa, Cotzin and Dallenbach tested blind and sighted people who walked towards a wall. When their ears were plugged, they bumped into it, even though the face was uncovered. When their faces were covered but their ears were free, they still stopped. They were hearing the echo of their own footsteps.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that some people sense objects with the skin of the face.

challenging.claim: Each pitch has its own stretched fibre in the cochlea, like a string on a piano.
challenging.who: Hermann von Helmholtz, a great German scientist, in 1863
challenging.for: Different places along the membrane do respond to different pitches, as the idea says.
challenging.against: In the 1940s Georg von Békésy looked at real cochleas and found no stretched strings. The membrane is soft, and sound makes a wave that travels along it and peaks at one place. The idea that each pitch has its own place was right. The strings were not.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous idea of how the ear sorts pitches that was partly right and partly wrong.

challenging.claim: Sign language is just gestures for spoken words, and not a real language.
challenging.who: Many hearing people for a long time
challenging.for: Signs can look like pictures of things, and some people think that means the language is simple.
challenging.against: Linguists since the 1960s have shown that sign languages have grammar, new words, jokes, poetry and dialects, and children learn them in the same stages as spoken languages. India has its own, Indian Sign Language.
challenging.context: This card is about whether sign languages are real languages.

challenging.claim: Tinnitus is always caused by damage in the ear.
challenging.for: It often starts after loud noise or hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells fit the pattern.
challenging.against: Some people with a cut hearing nerve still have tinnitus, and some people with healthy hearing hear it in a very quiet room. Many scientists now think the brain plays a large part.
challenging.context: This card is about where the ringing in tinnitus really comes from.

big_questions.q: Each ear only picks up how loud a sound is and the moment it arrives. Your brain works out where the sound is by comparing the two ears. So is the place of a sound out there in the room, or made inside you?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happened to your pointing in the Sound Clock when you covered one ear.

big_questions.q: Someone who is deaf in one ear and someone with two working ears sit in the same room. Do they hear the same room?
big_questions.hint: Think about which clues each of them has to build the place of a sound.

big_questions.q: In Hiding a Whisper, the whisper was still reaching your ears while the tap ran, but you could not hear it. Was the whisper there?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between a sound reaching you and a sound you hear.

big_questions.q: A moth hears a bat's call that no person can hear. If a sound is out there but nobody can hear it, is it still a sound?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether sound is a wave in the air or what a listener hears.

big_questions.q: In a noisy party, you can follow one voice and ignore the others. Who chooses what you hear: you, or your ears?
big_questions.hint: Think about how it feels to choose, and how you notice when someone says your name.

big_questions.q: Sign language uses no sound at all. Is it still a kind of listening?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens in the person who is watching.

big_questions.q: Silence is not the same as hearing nothing. In a quiet room many people hear a faint hiss. What are you hearing when it seems silent?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the ear and brain do when there is little sound to listen to.

big_questions.q: People across the world make music, which does nothing for food or safety. Why do you think hearing gives us such a strong feeling for it?
big_questions.hint: Think about drums, a lullaby and a song at a festival.

story.title: The Whistle at the Pooram
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Two ears use tiny differences in loudness and timing to find the direction of a sound. Turning the head helps tell front from back, because a sound in front moves the opposite way in your ears from a sound behind. A steady, thin whistle can be followed through loud drumming. The big festival in Thrissur, called the Pooram, really has rows of decorated elephants and large groups of drummers, but the girl and her family are invented.
text: Anjana was nine, and she had never seen so many people in one place. It was the day of the great festival in Thrissur. The whole town was packed around the temple ground, and the air smelled of jasmine and fried banana.

Her grandmother, Ammamma, held her hand tightly. Ammamma had been a teacher for forty years. Round her neck, on a red string, hung a steel whistle. She had used it for years to call children in from the playground.
"If we lose each other," said Ammamma, "stand still, and I will blow the whistle. Then walk towards it. Do not run."
A long row of elephants stood in the sun, dressed in gold. In front of them, a hundred drummers began to play. The chenda drums were so loud that Anjana felt the beat in her chest and in her teeth.
Then the crowd surged. A man pushed past with a big bunch of balloons, and Anjana's hand slipped out of her grandmother's.
She turned in a circle. There were faces, shoulders, flags, and balloons. There was no red string. "Ammamma!" she shouted. But the drums swallowed her voice. She could not even hear herself.
She stood still, as she had been told. Her heart was banging. The drums were so loud that she could not think.

Then, from far away, came a thin, bright sound. Peeeeep. It was the whistle. Anjana spun round. But the sound seemed to come from everywhere at once, from the temple wall, from the elephants and from the sky.
She ran towards where she thought it was. The whistle blew again, and now it seemed to come from behind her. She turned and ran the other way. It seemed to come from behind her again.

Anjana stopped. She was shaking. She tried to remember something. Last month, her teacher, Madam Lakshmi, had played a game in class. A girl sat with her eyes shut, and the class rang a small bell somewhere in the room. The girl had to point to it.

"You have two ears for a reason," Madam Lakshmi had said. "A sound reaches the nearer ear a tiny bit sooner and a tiny bit louder. Your brain compares the two. It works out the place without you even trying."
Anjana shut her eyes and held herself still. The whistle blew. It was a little louder in her right ear. She turned her head towards the right.

Peeeeep. Now it seemed to come equally to both ears. "Straight ahead," she whispered. "Or straight behind." She remembered the next part of the lesson. She turned her head a little to the left. The whistle moved to her right ear. "If it were behind me," she said, "it would have moved to my left. So it is in front."

She opened her eyes and walked a few steps. When the whistle was louder in one ear, she turned her head until it sounded the same in both. Then she walked on. Some steps she was wrong, but each time Ammamma blew, Anjana corrected her way.
The drums thundered. The whistle was thin and high, and so it did not drown. Each time it came, her ears could find it among the booming, like finding a bright thread in a dark cloth.

Ammamma stood on a step by the temple wall, looking in every direction. Then she saw a small girl walking in a straight line towards her, her head tilted a little to one side, like a bird listening for a worm.
Anjana ran the last few steps and put her arms round her grandmother. "I walked towards the whistle," she said. "I used both my ears."
"I did not think you would find me," said Ammamma. Her voice shook. "I thought I would have to stand here and blow all night. How did you do it?"
"The sound was louder on one side," said Anjana, "so I turned until it was the same on both. And when I could not tell front from back, I turned my head and watched which ear it moved to."
Ammamma looked at her for a long moment. "Madam Lakshmi," she said, smiling, "I owe you a box of sweets."

That night, at home, Anjana taught her little brother Kiran the game. He sat with his eyes shut in the middle of the room, and she rang the steel whistle from a different corner each time. Kiran pointed. Sometimes he was right, and sometimes he got front and back wrong. Anjana showed him how to turn his head.
story.epiphany: A sound does not tell you where it came from. Each ear only picks up how loud it is and the moment it arrives. The brain works out the direction by comparing the two ears. When both ears hear the same, the sound is straight ahead or straight behind, and turning the head tells which. A thin, steady sound is easier to follow through loud noise than a low sound.
ask: Why did the whistle seem to come from everywhere at first?
How did Anjana tell that a sound which reached both ears equally was in front of her?
Why was the thin whistle easier to follow than Anjana's own voice, when the drums were playing?
What could Ammamma have done to help Anjana find her even faster?

roots.context: We have tested how two ears find a sound, how noise hides a voice, and how the inner ear sorts pitches. Now we ask what these tests tell us about what a sound is, and about the person who hears it.

deep_truth.truth: Each ear only picks up how loud a sound is and the moment it arrives. Your brain works out 'left' or 'behind' from the difference between the two ears. In the Sound Clock, the same click seemed to come from somewhere else when one ear was covered. So where a sound is comes partly from the listener.
deep_truth.habit: We say a sound is over there, as if the place were inside the sound. A sound wave carries no label that says where it came from. The place is worked out by the listener from two ears.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sound Clock, pointing was good with two ears open and went wrong when one ear was covered, although the sound was exactly the same. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You hear the world through a head with two ears and a brain that compares them. Someone with one ear hears the same room, and builds the places of the sounds in a slightly different way.
three.what_is_life: A barn owl has ears at different heights, so she can tell above from below. A cricket hears with her front legs, and a mosquito with his antennae. Each kind of listener hears the world in a way that fits their own body.
three.what_is_this_world: A sound is a wave of squeezes in the air. It carries energy and a rhythm, but nothing in it says where it came from or how loud it will seem. The place and the loudness are worked out by the listener who hears it.

roots.thread: A sound spreads out from its source in every direction, and each ear catches only a tiny piece of it. The brain works out the direction from the difference between the two pieces. It works out the pitch from where the wave peaks along the coiled membrane in the cochlea. So what we hear depends on both the wave and the listener. The same wave reaches a bat, a moth or a person, and each one hears it differently.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad says that when a drum is beaten, one cannot grasp the sounds that go out from it, but by grasping the drum or the drummer, one grasps the sound.
teachings.link: You cannot get hold of a sound by itself. You find it through the drum, the air and the listener together.

teachings.teaching: Zhuangzi, an ancient Chinese thinker, described the wind blowing across ten thousand hollows in the earth, each one making its own sound. He asked who makes them sound, when the wind is the same.
teachings.link: The same wave sounds different in each ear and in each hollow, because the one who receives it shapes what is heard.

science.text: People can notice a difference of about one hundred-thousandth of a second between the ears, and use it to find the direction of a sound.
How the brain joins the clues from two ears, the shape of the pinna, head turns and the eyes into one place in space is not fully understood.

other_view.view: A sound has a place and a direction whether anyone hears it or not. The wave comes from the drum, and the drum is over there. The listener only finds the place, and does not make it.

practice.title: The sound sit
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Listen for one minute. Each time you hear a sound, point with one finger to where you think it is. Then turn your head slowly to the left, and notice how the sounds move to the right. Open your eyes and look at where the sounds were. Were you right?
practice.kid: Sit still. Shut your eyes. Listen for one minute. Point to each sound you hear. Then open your eyes. Were you right?

ask: If you had one ear, would you hear the same room?
When a bat's call is too high for you to hear, is there a sound in the room?
Where is the sound of a drum: in the drum, in the air, or in the listener?
roots.art: A girl sitting with her eyes closed and one hand pointing, with faint rings of sound reaching her from three sides, and a bat, an owl and a cricket outlined faintly behind her.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1863 the great German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz suggested that the inner ear works like a piano. He thought stretched fibres lay across the cochlea, short ones at one end and long ones at the other, and that each shook for one pitch like a string. It was a clever idea, and part of it was right: different places do answer to different pitches. In the 1920s and 1940s, a Hungarian scientist named Georg von Békésy looked at real ears. He studied ears from people who had died, because living ears are too small to look into. Under a microscope, he found no stretched strings. The membrane was soft. When he played a sound, he saw a wave travel along the membrane and rise to a peak at one place. High sounds peaked near the entrance, and low sounds near the far end. So the ear sorts pitches by where a wave peaks, not by strings. Békésy won the Nobel Prize in 1961.
how_we_found_out.who: Georg von Békésy (1899 to 1972), a Hungarian scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Helmholtz thought the cochlea had stretched fibres like piano strings, each shaking for one pitch. Békésy showed there were no stretched strings. A wave travels along a soft membrane and peaks at a place that depends on the pitch.

games.title: Decibel Ladder: how loud is it, and how long is it safe?
games.context: This is a card game about loud and quiet sounds. You guess how loud each sound is in decibels, place it on a ladder, and learn how long it is safe to listen.

printables.title: A ladder with 6 bands to draw on a big sheet of paper
items: 40 to 60 decibels: quiet to normal talk
60 to 80 decibels: loud, but safe for hours

rules: Cut out the cards and shuffle them in a pile with the sound side up. Draw the ladder with six bands on a big sheet of paper: 20 to 39, 40 to 59, 60 to 79, 80 to 99, 100 to 119, and 120 and up.
The first player picks up the top card and reads out the sound on the front. Do not turn the card over yet.
Everybody guesses which band of the ladder the sound belongs to, and says why.
Turn the card over and read the decibel number. Place the card on the right band of the ladder.
A player whose guess was in the right band gets one point. A player who guessed the band next door gets half a point.
Take turns to read cards. The game ends when all the cards are on the ladder.
At the end, look at the cards of 85 decibels and above. Put them in order of the safe time on the back, from the longest to the shortest.
If you play alone, guess each band before turning the card over, and try to score 20 or more out of 24.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and shuffle them. Draw the ladder with six bands on a big sheet of paper, with the quietest band at the bottom. Put the ladder in the middle of the table. Write the six bands on the ladder. They are 20 to 39, 40 to 59, 60 to 79, 80 to 99, 100 to 119 and 120 up.
flow.say: Each card has a sound on the front. On the back is how loud it is. We will guess how loud each sound is. Then we place it on a ladder, from quiet at the bottom to loud at the top.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Draw the ladder with six bands.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Decibel Ladder. You make the cards and the ladder.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 players, everyone guesses at once and keeps their own score. Take turns to read the cards. Playing alone works too.

flow.do: Take the whisper, the normal conversation and the firecracker cards. Place them on the ladder. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Here are three cards: a whisper, a normal conversation and a firecracker. Place each one on the ladder where you think it goes. Then we check the backs.
flow.kid: Place the whisper, the conversation and the firecracker on the ladder.

check.q: A whisper is about 30 decibels and a normal conversation is about 60 decibels. How much more sound energy does the conversation have?
options: 1,000 times as much
2 times as much
30 times as much
check.why: The conversation is 30 decibels higher, which is three steps of 10. Every step of 10 is 10 times the energy. 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000. If you picked 30 times, you subtracted 30 from 60 and used the result as the number of times.

flow.context: In this step, you place three cards to learn how the scale works.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards. For each, everyone guesses the band first. Then turn it over. Keep a score. After every six cards, ask the question below.
flow.say: Read the sound on the front. Guess the band. Then turn the card over and read the decibels. The right band scores one point. The band next door scores half a point.
flow.kid: Read a card. Guess the band. Turn it over. Place it on the ladder.

ask.q: Which sound surprised you most, and why?
good: Headphones turned up full, because I did not know they can be that loud.
The mosquito, because she is so tiny.
A city street, because it is louder than I thought.

flow.parent: Children often underestimate headphones and a mixer. Do not lecture. Let the numbers speak, and keep the score light.
flow.context: In this step, you play through the cards and score your guesses.

flow.do: Look at the finished ladder. Ask your child to point to the sounds that are safe all day and the sounds that need a time limit.
flow.say: Look at the finished ladder. Show me the sounds that are safe all day. Now show me the sounds that need a time limit.
flow.kid: Point to the sounds safe all day. Point to the ones with a time limit.
flow.parent: Sounds below about 80 decibels are safe all day. At 85 decibels and above, the safe time starts to shrink.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the cards into sounds that are safe all day and sounds that need a time limit.

flow.do: Take the cards of 85 decibels and above. Put them in order of the safe time on the back, from longest to shortest. Ask the question below, and let your child work it out before you say the answer.
flow.say: At 85 decibels the safe time is 8 hours. Each 3 decibels louder halves it. So how long is it safe at 100 decibels?
flow.kid: Each 3 decibels louder halves the safe time. How long is it safe at 100 decibels?

check.q: The safe time at 85 decibels is 8 hours, and every 3 decibels more halves it. About how long is it safe at 100 decibels?
options: About 15 minutes
About 4 hours
About 1 hour
check.why: 100 is 15 more than 85, which is five steps of 3 decibels. Halve 8 hours five times: 4 hours, 2 hours, 1 hour, 30 minutes, 15 minutes. If you picked 4 hours, you halved only once.

flow.context: In this step, you use the halving rule to find a safe time.

experiments.title: The Sound Clock: can you find a sound with one ear?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sit with your eyes shut while someone clinks a spoon in different places around you, and you point to each one. You do it with two ears and then with one ear covered.
experiments.question: How well can you find where a sound is with two ears, and how much worse is it with one ear covered?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Out of 16 clicks, how many will you point to exactly right with two ears, and how many with one ear covered? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same chair, the same spoon and katori, the same distance of 1.5 metres and the same eight places every time. Each place is clicked twice in each round, in a mixed-up order. Only the ears change. Keep your eyes shut or covered for every click. Keep your head still in Rounds A and B. Do it in the quietest room, with fans and the TV off.
results_table: My guess: how many exactly right out of 16?
Exactly right plus one place off

materials.item: a chair, placed in the middle of a clear floor space about 4 metres wide
a steel katori or a steel tumbler and a steel spoon, to make a sharp click
a scarf or a clean cloth to cover the eyes, or a sleeping mask
a soft ear cover, such as children's earmuffs, a thick woollen cap pulled over one ear, or a folded towel pressed on firmly by a helper. Earmuffs are optional
24 small paper slips: 8 marked Front, Front-right, Right, Back-right, Back, Back-left, Left and Front-left for the floor circle, and 16 more to draw from, two for each place
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never push cotton wool, earbuds or anything else into the ear. Clear the floor of anything to trip over before eyes are covered. Make each click gently and keep the katori at least 1 metre from the listener's head.

schedule.what: Do three rounds of 16 clicks: two ears, one ear covered, and two ears with head turns. Score each round and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three rounds. Then finish this sentence: 'With one ear covered, my pointing went ...'

flow.do: Show your child the chair, the katori and the eight places. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: I will click a spoon on a katori around you, and you will point to it with your eyes shut. First with two ears, then with one ear covered. How many out of 16 will you get exactly right each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will shut your eyes and point to each click. Guess how many you will get right. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think covering one ear will change your pointing?
good: One ear hears less, so I cannot tell where it is.
The sound will seem to come from the open side.
Two ears work like two eyes, so one makes it harder.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down, with the reason. Children often guess they will get most right with two ears, and some think one ear will not matter. Roles: one child listens, one clicks and one writes the scores. With 2 to 4 children, take turns as listener, with 8 clicks per round for each. Each listener keeps their own table and the same covered ear.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sound Clock. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the chair in the middle of a clear space. Lay the eight paper slips on the floor in a circle 1.5 metres from the chair, with Front straight ahead. Make a pile of 16 slips, two of each place, and shuffle them.
flow.say: The chair is the middle. The slips make a circle around it, 1.5 metres away. I will pick a slip, go to that place quietly, and click once. You will point and say where you think I am.
flow.kid: Sit on the chair. The slips make a circle around you. You will shut your eyes soon.
flow.parent: Wear soft socks so your footsteps do not give you away. Wait 3 seconds after reaching a place before you click. Pick the slips from a bag or a shuffled pile so the order is random. Write the true place and the pointed place for each click. Children may peek, so cover the eyes properly.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the chair and the circle of places.

flow.do: Cover your child's eyes. Draw a slip and move to that place quietly. Click once. Your child points and says where the click is, such as front, left or back. Write it down. Do all 16 slips. Your child keeps their head still.
flow.say: Keep your head still. When you hear the click, point with one finger and say where it is. Even if you are not sure, make a guess.
flow.kid: Eyes covered. Keep your head still. Point to each click.
flow.parent: Round A is two ears, head still. Mark each pointing as exactly right, one place off, or more than one place off. Front and back mix-ups count as more than one place off. Typically a child gets about 9 to 12 exactly right, plus a few front and back mix-ups. Your numbers will differ.

check.q: A click straight in front of your head and a click straight behind your head reach both ears together. Why are these two places the hardest to tell apart?
options: For both places, the sound reaches the two ears at the same time and equally loudly, so the main clues are the same
The click is quieter at the front and back
The ears cannot hear sounds at the front or back
check.why: A sound exactly in front or exactly behind is the same distance from both ears. The time and loudness clues are the same for both places. The folds of the ear and head turns are needed to tell them apart. If you chose 'The ears cannot hear sounds at the front or back', think about whether you can hear things in front of you.

flow.context: In this step, you do Round A: two ears open, head still.

flow.do: Now cover one ear with a soft cover. Shuffle the slips and do another 16 clicks. Keep the head still. Mark each one as before. Note which side most of the mistakes lean towards.
flow.say: This time one ear is covered. Same game. Keep your head still. Point when you hear the click. Do you think it will be harder or easier?
flow.kid: One ear is covered. Same game. Keep your head still.
flow.parent: Round B is one ear covered. Typically a child gets about 4 to 7 exactly right, though some children do better. If nothing changes, press the cover on harder and use a quieter room. Many wrong answers lean towards the open ear, because the sound seems louder there. If your child finds that sounds on the covered side seem to come from the front, that is normal. Remember: nothing goes inside the ear. Use an earmuff, a cap or a hand.
flow.context: In this step, you do Round B: one ear covered, head still.

flow.do: Take the ear cover off. Shuffle the slips and do a third round of 16 clicks. This time your child may turn the head from side to side while listening. Eyes stay covered.
flow.say: Back to two ears. This time you may turn your head from side to side as you listen. Does it help?
flow.kid: Two ears again. This time you may turn your head. Does it help?
flow.parent: Round C is two ears with head turns. Typically the front and back mix-ups drop a lot and 12 or more are exactly right. Results vary. When the head turns, a different ear becomes the one nearer the sound, and the brain uses the change.
flow.context: In this step, you do Round C: two ears, head turns allowed.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What numbers show it? And why do you think it happened? What did turning your head do?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.

check.q: In Round A of the Sound Clock you had two ears open. In Round B one ear was covered, and the same clicks made you point wrongly. What changed between the rounds?
options: Only the clues your brain got, because with one ear covered it had nothing to compare
The clicks got quieter
The room changed
check.why: The clicks and the room were the same. With one ear covered the brain no longer had two ears to compare, so it could not use the time and loudness differences. If you chose 'The clicks got quieter', remember that each click was made in the same way.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'With two ears I was right a lot. With one ear covered I made many more mistakes. I think the brain finds where a sound is by comparing what the two ears hear. When I could turn my head, I got even better, because the head turn changed what the ears heard.' Now read the card 'Two ears tell where a sound is'.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, with evidence and a reason.

experiments.title: Hiding a Whisper: how far can a whisper reach in noise?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up whispers numbers from different distances, first in a quiet room and then with a tap running. You find out how far a whisper reaches each time.
experiments.question: How much shorter is the distance a whisper reaches when there is noise, and what can a speaker do to be heard?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How far will a whisper reach in a quiet room? How far with a tap running gently? How far with the tap running hard? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The listener sits in the same place with eyes shut for every test. The whisperer uses the same quiet whisper for every digit. Only the noise changes. Five digits are whispered at each distance, picked in a mixed-up order. A distance counts as heard if the listener gets at least 4 of the 5 right. The whisperer practises one steady whisper at 1 metre first. Fans and the TV are off, except the noise being tested.
results_table: My guess: how far will a whisper reach? (metres)

materials.item: a long clear space of at least 6 metres, such as a corridor or a hall, with marks at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres in tape or paper slips. No 6 metres? Use a terrace, a stair landing or a quiet lane
a chair for the listener, a scarf to cover the eyes
a steady noise: a tap running into a steel bucket (keep the water for the plants), or a table fan on high, or a phone playing a steady rain or crowd track at a fixed volume
a list of digits from 0 to 9, written in a mixed-up order, 5 for each distance and each round
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do not make the noise louder than a loud conversation, so that nobody has to shout and nobody's ears are hurt. Wipe up water at once.

schedule.what: Whisper digits from 1 to 5 metres in a quiet room, with a gentle tap and with a hard tap. Find how far the whisper reaches each time, then test what helps.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then finish this sentence: 'The louder the noise, the ...' and write one thing that helped a whisper be heard.

flow.do: Show your child the corridor, the tap and the list of digits. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: I will whisper numbers to you from different distances. First in a quiet room. Then with a tap running gently. Then with it running hard. How far will my whisper reach each time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how far a whisper will reach in quiet, and in noise. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the noise will change how far the whisper reaches?
good: The noise is louder than the whisper, so it covers it.
I will have to listen harder.
The whisper will still arrive, but I won't be able to hear it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A whisper is about 30 decibels. In a quiet room it often reaches 4 or 5 metres. Write the guess in metres. Roles: one child listens, one whispers and one records. Keep the same listener for all the tests so they are fair. With 2 to 4 children, swap listeners on another day, or repeat only the quiet round.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hiding a Whisper. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Mark 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres along the floor from the listener's chair. Write the digit lists. If the room has a tap, put the bucket under it. If not, get a fan or a phone with a rain track ready.
flow.say: We mark the floor at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres from the chair. For each distance I will whisper five digits. I have written them down in a mixed-up order.
flow.kid: Mark the floor at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres. Sit on the chair.
flow.parent: If your tap is not in the same room, use a table fan on its highest setting, or a phone playing a steady rain or crowd track at a fixed volume, as your loud noise. Put the noise source near the listener, about 1.5 metres to one side. Make sure the noise is steady. The listener keeps eyes covered.
flow.context: In this step, you mark the distances and get the noise ready.

flow.do: Do the quiet round first. Stand at 1 metre. Whisper five digits one at a time. The listener says each digit. Write down how many are right. Then move to 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres.
flow.say: Listen carefully. I will whisper a number. Say it back. If you don't hear it, take a guess. We start with a quiet room.
flow.kid: Eyes covered. Listen for each number. Say it back. Guess if unsure.
flow.parent: Whisper clearly but quietly, always the same way. Stop moving back when the listener gets fewer than 4 of 5 right. The furthest distance with 4 or 5 right is the whisper reach. Typically 3 to 5 metres in a quiet room. A small room, hard walls or street noise will change this.

check.q: Why do we whisper five digits at each distance, and not just one?
options: One lucky guess could fool us, so we need several tries
To make the test longer
Because five is the right number for whispers
check.why: A digit can be guessed right by luck, one time in ten. Five digits make a lucky run very unlikely. If you picked 'To make the test longer', remember that a test is not better just because it is longer. More tries make it fairer.

flow.context: In this step, you find how far a whisper reaches in a quiet room.

flow.do: Turn on the tap gently, with a steady trickle into the bucket. Repeat the whispers at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres. Then turn the tap on hard and repeat. Write the scores.
flow.say: Now the tap runs gently. Same whispers, same places. Listen and say the number. Then we will turn the tap up and do it again.
flow.kid: The tap is running. Listen for each number. Say it back.
flow.parent: Typically the whisper reaches less far with the tap running gently, about 2 or 3 metres, and much less with the tap running hard, about 1 metre or less. Your numbers will differ. If the whisper cannot be heard even at 1 metre, move to half a metre and write it beside the table. The whisper is still reaching the ear. It is hidden by the noise.
flow.context: In this step, you find how far a whisper reaches in two levels of noise.

flow.do: Keep the tap running hard. Stand at a distance where the listener got fewer than 4 right. Try two helps in turn. First, let the listener take off the scarf that covers their eyes and watch your mouth. Second, move one step closer.
flow.say: We are going to help the whisper get through the noise. First, you watch my mouth while I whisper. Then I come one step closer. Which helps more?
flow.kid: Watch the whisperer's mouth. Then try one step closer. Which helps more?
flow.parent: Seeing the lips usually helps a lot, because the brain uses the movements of the mouth to fill in what the ear misses. Moving closer helps too. Ask your child which one they would pick if they could pick only one in a noisy hall.
flow.context: In this step, you test two ways to help a quiet sound get heard in noise.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What numbers show it? And why do you think it happened? Was the whisper still arriving when the tap was loud?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.

check.q: With the tap running hard, you could not hear the whisper. What is the best explanation?
options: The whisper still reached your ear, but the louder noise hid it
The whisper stopped before it reached your ear
Your ear stopped working while the tap ran
check.why: The whisper was the same, and it still arrived. The louder tap sound moved the same part of the ear as the whisper, so the whisper was lost inside it. This is called masking. If you chose 'Your ear stopped working while the tap ran', notice that when the tap was turned off, you could hear the whisper again.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'The louder the noise, the shorter the distance a whisper reached. In a quiet room it reached about 4 metres. With the tap hard it reached less than 1 metre. I think the noise hid the whisper, even though it still reached my ear. Watching the lips and moving closer helped.' Now read the card 'Masking: why noise hides a voice'.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, with evidence and a reason.

experiments.title: Doubling the Distance: how fast does a sound fade as you move away?
experiments.context: In this experiment you measure how loud a steady sound is at four distances with a free sound meter app, and find what happens each time you double the distance.
experiments.question: Each time you double your distance from a steady sound, how many decibels does it drop?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If the fan reads 60 decibels at 1 metre, what will it read at 2 metres, 4 metres and 8 metres? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same sound on the same setting, the same phone and app, and the same height, one metre from the floor, for every reading. Only the distance changes. Take three readings at each distance and use the middle one, because the number on the app jumps around.

materials.item: a steady sound that stays the same for a few minutes: a table fan on high, or a phone or speaker playing a steady white-noise or rain track at a fixed volume
a phone with a free sound level meter app (search the app store for 'sound meter' or 'decibel meter')
a tape measure or a metre stick
a long room or corridor with 8 metres of clear floor
tape or paper slips to mark 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 metres
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep the sound no louder than a normal conversation. Use a fan with a guard, and keep fingers away from the blades. Switch off the fan when you finish.

schedule.what: Read the sound level of a steady fan at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 metres. Find the drop each time the distance doubles.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then work out the drop in decibels each time the distance doubled. Finish this sentence: 'Each time I doubled the distance, the sound dropped by about ...'

flow.do: Show your child the fan and the app. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table for each distance.
flow.say: We will measure the sound of the fan at four distances. If it reads 60 decibels at 1 metre, what will it read at 2 metres? At 4 metres? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how loud the fan is when you double the distance. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the sound will get quieter in that way?
good: It gets half as loud each time.
It drops by the same amount each time.
It spreads out as it goes.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess halving, so 30 decibels at 2 metres. Write each guess in the table. Roles: one child holds the phone, one reads the number and one writes. With one child, the parent writes. If no app is available, borrow a phone.
flow.context: This is the first step of Doubling the Distance. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Put the fan on a table at one end of the room. Switch it on at a steady speed. On the floor, mark 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 metres from the fan. Mark them along a line that runs out to the side of the fan, so that the fan's wind does not blow on the phone. Open the app and check that it reads a number.
flow.say: We place the fan at one end. We mark 0.5 metres, 1 metre, 2 metres and 4 metres along the floor. Then we open the app and check that it works.
flow.kid: Switch on the fan. Mark the floor at four distances. Open the app.
flow.parent: Phone microphones are not accurate. The numbers may be off by 5 decibels or more, and some apps do not read below 30 or above 90. That is fine here. We are looking at how the number changes between distances, not at the exact number. Hold the phone at the height of the fan, pointing at it, and do not move it between readings. Wind on the microphone makes false readings, so keep the phone out of the airflow. If the readings stop falling at about 40 decibels, the room noise is in the way. Turn off other noise, close the window, try at night, or play a louder track.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the fan, the distances and the app.

flow.do: Hold the phone at 0.5 metres, facing the fan. Wait 10 seconds. Read the number and write it down. Do this three times. Then do the same at 1, 2 and 4 metres.
flow.say: Hold the phone steady, pointing at the fan. Wait ten seconds for the number to settle. Read it and write it down. Three readings at each distance.
flow.kid: Hold the phone steady. Wait ten seconds. Read the number. Write it down.
flow.parent: Typical readings might be 62, 57, 53 and 49 decibels for 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 metres in a room. Yours will differ. The drops will not be the same each time. In a room with walls, sound bounces back, so each doubling drops about 3 to 5 decibels. In open air it is about 6.

check.q: At 1 metre the fan reads 57 decibels. At 2 metres it reads 53 decibels. What is the drop?
options: 4 decibels
110 decibels
Half of 57
check.why: The drop is 57 take away 53, which is 4 decibels. Adding the numbers to get 110 is a slip. Half of 57 would be a drop of nearly 29 decibels, much more than anything you measured.

flow.context: In this step, you take three readings at each of four distances.

flow.do: Put the three readings in order at each distance, and pick the middle one. Work out the drop from one distance to the next. Look for a pattern.
flow.say: For each distance, put the three readings in order and pick the middle one. Then subtract each middle reading from the one at the distance before it. What is the drop each time you double the distance?
flow.kid: Pick the middle reading. Find the drop each time the distance doubles.
flow.parent: The drops are likely to be similar to each other, around 3 to 6 decibels. In open air, sound spreads over a ball that gets four times bigger in area each time the distance doubles, so each bit gets a quarter of the energy, which is a drop of about 6 decibels.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the drop at each doubling.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say three things: what they think now, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What numbers show it? And why do you think it happened? Where does the sound's energy go as you move away?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.

check.q: Why does a sound get quieter as you move away from it?
options: The same energy spreads over a bigger and bigger area, so each part gets less
The sound gets tired as it travels
The air in the middle swallows the sound
check.why: Sound spreads out in every direction, like a ring of ripples that gets longer. The same energy covers a bigger area, so each bit has less. Picking 'the sound gets tired' is natural, but sound is not a living thing, and nothing is used up. It is spread thin.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'Every time I doubled the distance, the number dropped by about 4. It was not halving. I think the sound spreads out in all directions, so there is less in each place.' Now read the card 'Why a sound gets fainter as you move away'.
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found, with evidence and a reason.
