activities.title: Sound Map: eyes shut, point and draw
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You sit with your eyes shut, point to every sound you hear, and then draw a map of where the sounds were.

materials.item: a chair in the middle of a room, or a mat on the floor
a big sheet of paper with a circle drawn on it, and a small dot in the middle
a pencil
a scarf to cover the eyes, if the eyes will not stay shut

schedule.what: Listen with your eyes shut for two minutes. Point to each sound. Draw an arrow on the map for each one. Open your eyes and check.

activities.record: A circle map with the child at the dot. Arrows and names for each sound, and a tick or a cross for each one the child got right.

flow.do: Sit your child on the chair in the middle of the room. Show them the circle map. Explain that the dot is them, and the top of the paper is straight ahead. Ask them to guess how many sounds they will hear in two minutes.
flow.say: This map is of the room. The dot in the middle is you. The top of the page is straight ahead. In two minutes with your eyes shut, how many different sounds do you think you will hear? Which will be easiest to find?
flow.kid: The dot is you. The top is straight ahead. Guess how many sounds you will hear.

ask.q: Which sound do you think will be hardest to find the place of?
good: A quiet one, far away.
The fridge, because it hums all the time.
One from behind me.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. A city flat is never silent. Expect a fan, a fridge, a vehicle, a voice, a bird, a pressure cooker and a neighbour. With 2 to 4 children, each draws their own map in silence, then you compare maps. With one child, the parent draws.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sound Map. You guess before you listen.

flow.do: Ask your child to shut their eyes and sit very still for two minutes. Each time they hear a sound, they point to it and whisper what it is. Draw an arrow on the map, and write its name.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Sit very still. Every time you hear a sound, point to it and tell me what it is. I will draw it on the map.
flow.kid: Eyes shut. Sit still. Point to each sound. Say what it is.
flow.parent: Say nothing yourself, and keep your pencil quiet. Draw each arrow in the direction the child points. Write the name beside it. Do not tell them whether they are right yet.
flow.context: In this step, you listen for two minutes and mark each sound on the map.

flow.do: Open your eyes. Go to each sound with your child, and see where it really came from. Put a tick on the map if the arrow pointed within a hand's width of the real place. Otherwise put a cross.
flow.say: Now open your eyes. Let's walk to each sound and see where it really was. Was your finger pointing the right way? Which were easy? Which were hard?
flow.kid: Open your eyes. Walk to each sound. Was your finger right?
flow.parent: Steady humming sounds, such as a fridge or a fan, are usually harder to place than short sounds, such as a clink. Sounds behind and above are also harder.

check.q: Which kind of sound is usually hardest to find the place of with your eyes shut?
options: A steady hum, such as a fridge
A short sharp click
A voice calling your name
check.why: A steady, low hum gives the brain few clues about time, because there is no start to compare between the two ears. A sharp click has a clear start that reaches one ear before the other. If you picked the click, notice that a click was probably the easiest one on your map.

flow.context: In this step, you check your map against the real places.

flow.do: Look at the map together. Count how many sounds were behind and how many in front. Ask the question below, and let your child answer before you say anything.
flow.say: Look at the map. Which sounds were behind you? Which in front? Did you get more of the front ones right? Why do you think that might be?
flow.kid: Count the sounds in front. Count the sounds behind. Which were easier?
flow.think: Why might sounds from the front be easier to find than sounds from behind?
flow.parent: Most children find sounds on the left and right easiest, and front and behind harder. In the Sound Clock experiment, you will find out why.

activities.title: The Paper Snail: build a model of the cochlea
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper strip that is a model of the basilar membrane, and mark where the high and low pitches peak along it.

materials.item: chart paper or thin card cut into a strip at least 36 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide, or two A4 sheets taped end to end
a ruler and a pencil
a pair of scissors
cello tape
coloured pens for marking the pitches

schedule.what: Cut a strip that is narrow at one end and wide at the other. Mark where six pitches peak. Curl the strip into a snail.

activities.record: The strip with six marked pitches and the curled snail. Write under it: 'High pitches peak near the ... end. Low pitches peak near the ... end.'

flow.do: Draw a strip 35 centimetres long. Make one end 1 centimetre wide and the other end 5 centimetres wide. Join the sides with straight lines. Cut it out.
flow.say: The cochlea is a coiled tube about 3.5 centimetres long. Our model is 10 times as long, so 35 centimetres. The strip stands for the basilar membrane. It is narrow at one end and about five times wider at the other.
flow.kid: Draw a strip 35 centimetres long. Make one end 1 centimetre wide and the other end 5 centimetres wide.
flow.parent: Use the ruler to mark both ends and join them with straight lines. The narrow end is where the sound enters the cochlea. The wide end is deep inside. Real cochleas are tiny, so our model is ten times bigger than life in length. With 2 to 4 children, each makes a strip. Share one ruler and one pair of scissors.

check.q: The cochlea is about 35 millimetres long when unrolled. Our model is 10 times as long. How long is our model?
options: 350 millimetres, which is 35 centimetres
45 millimetres
3.5 millimetres
check.why: 35 millimetres times 10 is 350 millimetres. There are 10 millimetres in a centimetre, so that is 35 centimetres. Adding 10 instead of multiplying is the usual slip.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Snail. You cut out the model of the basilar membrane.

flow.do: Mark the strip with a ruler from the narrow end. At 0 centimetres write 20,000 hertz. At 7 write 8,000. At 14 write 3,000. At 21 write 1,000. At 28 write 300. At 35 write 20.
flow.say: Each mark shows where a sound of that pitch makes the wave peak. The narrow end is for the highest sounds. The wide end is for the lowest. A police whistle is about 3,000 hertz, so it peaks at 14 centimetres.
flow.kid: Mark the pitches along the strip. High at the narrow end. Low at the wide end.
flow.parent: These marks are rounded from measurements of the human cochlea. A bat's squeak at 50,000 hertz is off the narrow end, so humans do not hear it. A deep drum at 100 hertz is near the wide end. Colour the high end red and the low end blue.

check.q: Where on the strip would a very high whistle make the wave peak?
options: Near the narrow end
Near the wide end
In the exact middle
check.why: High pitches peak near the narrow, stiff start of the membrane. Low pitches peak near the wide, soft end. If you picked the wide end, you may have mixed up the two ends.

flow.context: In this step, you mark where six pitches peak along the membrane.

flow.do: Draw a wave on the strip that peaks at the 14 centimetre mark. Draw a second wave in another colour that peaks at the 28 centimetre mark. Label each with a sound it could be. Then guess where 5,000 hertz would go, and mark it with a dot.
flow.say: A police whistle makes a wave that peaks at 14 centimetres. Draw it on the strip. A low voice at about 300 hertz peaks at 28 centimetres. Draw that too, in another colour.
flow.kid: Draw a wave that peaks at 14 centimetres. Draw another that peaks at 28.
flow.parent: A real wave starts at the narrow end, grows bigger as it travels, then rises to a peak and dies away very fast just past the peak. The hair cells at the peak are the ones that signal strongly. Draw the wave as a bump that grows and then drops. The 5,000 hertz dot belongs at about 10 centimetres, between the 8,000 and 3,000 marks. Check your guess against it.
flow.context: In this step, you draw two travelling waves on the strip.

flow.do: Curl the strip into a snail, with the narrow end on the outside. Tape it so it stays curled. Count the turns. Real cochleas have about two and a half turns.
flow.say: Real cochleas are coiled up like a snail to fit inside the head. Curl your strip with the narrow end on the outside. Wrap it round two or three times.
flow.kid: Curl the strip into a snail. Narrow end outside. Tape it.
flow.parent: The paper snail will not curl perfectly. It does not need to. The point is to see how a 3.5 centimetre tube can fit into a space the size of a pea. The coil shape does not change how the wave travels.

activities.title: Feel the Music: a balloon and a drum beat
activities.context: In this activity you feel sound through your hands and skin, as many Deaf musicians do, and find out which sounds you can feel best.

materials.item: a round balloon, blown up
a speaker with real bass, such as a Bluetooth speaker, a TV or a music system. A phone speaker is too small to make low notes you can feel
a table or the floor
a scarf or a quiet pair of earmuffs to cover the ears, if you want to try without hearing

activities.safety: Keep the music at the loudness of a normal conversation. Do not press the balloon hard against a speaker cone, because it can burst. If anyone is allergic to latex, use a paper cup or a plastic tub with cling film stretched over the top instead. Pick up burst balloon pieces at once, and keep them away from small children. An adult blows up the balloons for children under 8.

schedule.what: Hold a balloon near a speaker playing a drum beat. Feel the beat. Hum against the balloon. Compare low and high sounds.

activities.record: Draw the balloon and write down which sounds you could feel the most: a low drum, a high whistle, or your own humming. Give each sound a score from 0 (nothing) to 5 (buzzes strongly).

flow.do: Show your child the balloon and the speaker. Ask them to guess whether they can feel sound with their hands, and which sounds they will feel the most.
flow.say: Sound is a wave in the air. If a wave is strong enough, we can feel it with our skin. Do you think we can feel sound with our hands? Which sounds, low drums or high whistles? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Can you feel music with your hands? Which sounds? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which sounds do you think you will feel the most, and why?
good: Low drum sounds, because they shake more.
Loud ones, because they push the air hard.
High whistles, because they are sharp.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. With 2 to 4 children, each holds a balloon and scores the sounds. Then compare scores.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel the Music. You guess before you feel.

flow.do: Play music with a clear drum beat at conversation volume. Hold the balloon in both hands, about a hand's width from the speaker. Feel the beat on the balloon. Then try a high tune, such as a flute or a whistle.
flow.say: Hold the balloon lightly in both hands, close to the speaker. Play a song with a deep drum. What do you feel on your hands? Now play something high, such as a flute. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Hold the balloon near the speaker. Feel a drum beat. Then feel a high tune.
flow.parent: The balloon thumps clearly with deep drum notes and hardly at all with high flute notes. Low sounds shake the air in big, slow pushes that the skin can feel. If you feel nothing, turn up the volume to a little louder than a conversation, but no more. Still nothing? Rest the balloon lightly on top of the speaker box, not on the cone.

check.q: Which sound is easiest to feel with your hands on a balloon?
options: A deep drum beat
A high flute note
They feel the same
check.why: Slow, strong pushes from a deep drum are easiest for the skin to sense. High flute notes shake the air too fast for the balloon and skin to follow. If you picked 'They feel the same', try both again, and focus on your fingertips.

flow.context: In this step, you feel a drum beat and a flute through a balloon.

flow.do: Hold the balloon against your cheek and hum a low note, then a high note. Feel which one buzzes more. Then put your fingers on your throat and do the same. Ask your child what they notice.
flow.say: Press the balloon to your cheek and hum a low note. Then hum a high note. Which buzzes more? Now touch your throat and hum again. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Hum a low note against the balloon. Then a high note. Which buzzes more?
flow.think: Evelyn Glennie, a percussionist who cannot hear well, plays barefoot to feel the music through the floor. Why would feet be good for feeling low sounds?
flow.parent: A low hum buzzes a lot more on the cheek than a high hum. Glennie plays without shoes so she can feel the beats and low notes through the floor and her whole body. She says she hears with her whole body, not only with her ears.

setup.caption: 1. Hold the balloon near a speaker playing a drum beat.

setup.art: A child pressing a balloon against her cheek while humming, with small wave lines near her mouth.
setup.caption: 2. Press the balloon to your cheek and hum a low note, then a high note.

activities.title: Stand Like a Flamingo: your ears help you balance
activities.context: In this activity you stand on one leg with your eyes open and then shut, and find out how your eyes, feet and inner ears work together to keep you balanced.

materials.item: a stopwatch or a phone stopwatch
a soft mat or a folded blanket on the floor, next to a wall
a pencil and paper for a table

activities.safety: Stand next to a wall or a sturdy table so that you can touch it if you start to fall. Stop if you feel dizzy. Clear the floor of toys and sharp corners. A grown-up stays within arm's reach when the child's eyes are shut.

schedule.what: Time how long you can stand on one leg with your eyes open and then with your eyes shut. Compare.

activities.record: A table with two rows: eyes open and eyes shut. For each, write three times in seconds and the longest.

flow.do: Show your child how to stand on one leg, with the other foot lifted and the arms free, next to the wall. Ask them to guess which will be longer, eyes open or eyes shut, and why.
flow.say: We will time how long you can stand on one leg. First with your eyes open, then with your eyes shut. Which do you think will be longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand on one leg. Eyes open or eyes shut? Which lasts longer? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think shutting your eyes will change how long you can stand?
good: Because I can't see where I'm leaning.
Because my eyes help me balance.
It won't change, because balance is in the legs.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. Roles: one stands, one times and one writes. Swap after each child has had their turns.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stand Like a Flamingo. You guess before you try.

flow.do: Time your child standing on one leg with their eyes open. Stop the clock if the lifted foot touches down or they touch the wall. Stop at 30 seconds. Do it three times, then swap legs and do it again.
flow.say: Stand next to the wall, on one leg, with your eyes open. I will time you. Stop if your foot touches down. We stop at 30 seconds. Three tries, and then the other leg.
flow.kid: Stand on one leg, eyes open. Stop when your foot touches down.
flow.parent: Most children can manage 30 seconds with eyes open. Hold the stopwatch where your child cannot see it, so that they are not distracted. Write down each time.
flow.context: In this step, you time standing on one leg with your eyes open.

flow.do: Now ask your child to shut their eyes, and time them again, three tries on each leg. Stay close, and be ready to catch them. Stop the clock if the foot touches down.
flow.say: Now shut your eyes. Stand on one leg. I will be right beside you. Stop if you wobble too much. Three tries on each leg.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Stand on one leg. Stop if you wobble too much.
flow.parent: Typically the time drops a lot, often to 5 to 15 seconds. Some children manage more. With the eyes shut, the brain has lost one of its three sources of balance information. The inner ear and the feet are still working. Standing on a soft mat makes it harder, because the feet feel less.

check.q: Shutting your eyes made standing on one leg harder. What is the best explanation?
options: The eyes are one of the three things that tell the brain about balance
The legs got weaker when the eyes shut
The floor became less flat
check.why: Balance uses the eyes, the inner ears and the feel of the feet together. With the eyes shut, the brain has only two sources left, so it manages less well. If you picked 'The legs got weaker when the eyes shut', notice that your legs were just as strong a moment before.

flow.context: In this step, you time standing on one leg with your eyes shut.

setup.caption: 1. Stand on one leg beside a wall. Eyes open first.

setup.art: The same child with her eyes shut, wobbling, with a parent standing close.
setup.caption: 2. Now shut your eyes and stand on one leg again.

activities.title: Ten Signs: a first lesson in Indian Sign Language
activities.context: In this activity you try a short conversation with no sound, then learn a few signs from Indian Sign Language, to feel what talking without hearing is like.

materials.item: a phone, tablet or computer with the internet
a parent or friend to practise with
a pencil and paper to note the signs

schedule.what: Chat for one minute with no sound. Then watch a short lesson in Indian Sign Language, learn a few signs, and use them in a silent chat.

activities.record: A list of the signs you learned, with a drawing or a note of how each one looks, and one thing you noticed about talking without sound.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell you what they ate for breakfast, with no sound at all, for one minute. They can use their hands, face and body. Then swap.
flow.say: For one minute, tell me what you had for breakfast, with no sound at all. You can use your hands, your face and your body. I will guess.
flow.kid: Tell me about breakfast with no sound. Use your hands and face.

ask.q: What was hardest about talking with no sound?
good: I could not say the names of foods.
I had to use my face a lot.
It took much longer.

flow.parent: This is mime, which is not the same as a sign language. It shows how much meaning hands and faces can carry. A real sign language is far richer. Count how many breakfast items were guessed right in the minute. With 2 to 4 children, take turns as signer and guessers.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Signs. You try a silent chat.

flow.do: Find the website of the Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre, islrtc.nic.in, or its YouTube channel. Or search for a short beginners lesson. Watch it with your child. Learn to sign a greeting and your own names.
flow.say: Indian Sign Language is a real language, with its own words and grammar. Let's watch a short lesson from the Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre. We will learn a greeting and try to sign our names.
flow.kid: Watch a short lesson in Indian Sign Language. Copy a greeting and your name.
flow.parent: Watch the video yourself first, and choose a short lesson for beginners. Many signs use both hands and the face. In sign languages, the face and the speed of the hands add meaning, just as the tone of the voice does in speech. If you do not have the internet, try the finger-spelling chart in a library book. Respect the language: a Deaf person is the best teacher.

check.q: Which statement about sign languages is true?
options: They are full languages with their own grammar
They are only gestures that copy spoken words
They are the same in every country
check.why: Linguists have shown that sign languages have their own grammar, new words, jokes and poems. Different countries have different sign languages. India has its own, called Indian Sign Language.

flow.context: In this step, you watch a short lesson and learn a few signs.

flow.do: Use the signs you learned for a short silent chat. Greet each other, sign your names, and say goodbye. Then talk about what it felt like.
flow.say: Let's greet each other with the signs we learned, and tell each other our names. How did it feel? Which part was easy? Which part was hard?
flow.kid: Greet each other in signs. Sign your names. Say goodbye.
flow.think: If you had a friend who could not hear, what could you do to make talking together easier?
flow.parent: Good answers include: face them, keep your mouth visible, speak clearly without shouting, cut down the noise, write or use signs, and be patient. Learning a few signs is a real kindness to a Deaf friend.

projects.title: Ear Trumpets: does a bigger mouth hear more?
projects.context: In this 2-day project you make paper ear trumpets with three sizes of opening, and find out how far away you can hear a very quiet sound with each.

materials.item: 3 sheets of chart paper or thin card, each at least 30 centimetres on each side (A4 is too small for the 20 centimetre mouth)
cello tape, a pair of scissors and a ruler
a phone playing a very quiet steady high beep from a free tone generator app (about 2,000 to 4,000 hertz) or a video of a steady tone, or a metronome click
a long corridor, hall or terrace of at least 8 metres, with tape marks every metre. With no such space, keep a fixed distance of 3 metres and turn the phone volume down step by step instead
a scarf to cover the eyes
a pencil and a sheet of paper for the table

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the card. The small end of the trumpet rests near the ear, never pushed in. Keep the sound quiet. Never use a trumpet near loud sounds, and never shout into one.

schedule.what: Make three ear trumpets, with mouths of about 5, 10 and 20 centimetres. Test how far away you can hear a quiet beep with no trumpet and with each trumpet.
Test the trumpets pointed at the sound and pointed the wrong way. Draw a bar chart of the distances, and explain the result.

projects.record: Day 1: a table of the distance at which the beep faded for no trumpet and each trumpet. Day 2: a bar chart, and a sentence saying which trumpet was best and why.

flow.do: Show your child the paper, the phone and the corridor. Ask which size of trumpet mouth will let them hear furthest, and why.
flow.say: Long ago, before hearing aids, people used ear trumpets to hear better. Today we make three. The mouth of a trumpet is its wide, open end. One trumpet has a small mouth, one a medium mouth and one a big mouth. Which do you think will help most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We make three ear trumpets. Which size of mouth helps you hear furthest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that size will help the most?
good: The bigger mouth catches more sound.
A small mouth sends the sound straight in.
They will all be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it down. The ear flap on the side of the head is itself a small natural ear trumpet. Roles: one listens, one walks with the phone and one measures and writes. With 2 to 4 children, keep one listener for the whole test, or each child makes a trumpet and tests alone.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ear Trumpets. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Roll each sheet into a cone. Make the mouths about 5 centimetres, 10 centimetres and 20 centimetres wide. Leave the small end about 1.5 centimetres wide. Tape each cone. Trim the small end so it is not sharp.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts and rolls the card. Each cone has a big opening and a small end. The small end is for your ear, and the big opening is for catching sound. Make three, with big openings of different sizes.
flow.kid: Roll three cones of different sizes. The small end goes near your ear.
flow.parent: Roll each sheet from a corner. A 30 centimetre square gives a mouth of about 20 centimetres. Roll tighter for the smaller mouths, then trim all three to about 25 centimetres long. Make the mouth sizes clearly different: about 5, 10 and 20 centimetres across. Keep the cones the same length, about 25 centimetres, if you can. Label them S, M and L. Check that the small end is smooth and comfortable.
flow.context: In this step, you make three ear trumpets.

flow.do: Set the phone to a very quiet beep. The listener sits at one end of the corridor with eyes covered. The grown-up walks away slowly with the phone. The listener raises a hand when the beep fades. Measure the distance. Repeat with each trumpet held to one ear.
flow.say: Keep your eyes covered. Listen to the beep as I walk away. Raise your hand the moment you can't hear it. We will do it with no trumpet, then with each trumpet.
flow.kid: Eyes covered. Raise your hand when the beep fades. Do it with each trumpet.
flow.parent: Keep the phone at the same volume and the same height each time. Walk at a steady pace. Do each trumpet twice and write down both distances. Hold the trumpet's wide opening pointing toward the sound, with the narrow end near, not in, the ear. Typically the big trumpet adds a metre or two, but the difference can be small and it varies. Test in a quiet place with fans off, and point the phone speaker at the listener. If there is no difference, say so honestly. A paper trumpet is a weak amplifier.

check.q: Why must the beep stay at exactly the same volume for every test?
options: So that only the trumpet changes
So that the beep sounds better
So that the corridor stays quiet
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes at a time. If the volume changed, you could not tell whether the trumpet or the volume made the difference.

flow.context: On day 1, you test how far you can hear a quiet beep with each trumpet.

flow.do: Test the large trumpet again, but this time point it away from the sound. Compare the distance with the distance when it points toward the sound.
flow.say: Today we try one more thing. Hold the big trumpet so its wide mouth points away from the beep. How far can you hear it now? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Point the big trumpet away from the beep. How far can you hear?
flow.parent: Typically the distance drops, perhaps to less than with no trumpet. The wide mouth collects sound only from the direction it faces. This is why the ear flap faces forward and why many animals can turn their ears.
flow.context: On day 2, you test what happens when the trumpet points the wrong way.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with the trumpets along the bottom: none, small, medium, large, large pointed away. Draw a bar for each distance. Ask your child to say which was best and why.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each distance. Which trumpet was best? Which was worst? Why do you think the wide mouth helped?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each trumpet. Which is tallest? Why?

check.q: A wider ear trumpet lets you hear a quiet sound from further away. What does the wide mouth do?
options: It collects more of the sound and sends it into the ear
It makes the sound louder at the source
It stops other sounds from reaching the ear
check.why: A wide mouth catches a bigger share of the spreading sound and guides it to a small opening at the ear. The trumpet does not add energy. It gathers energy that would have missed the ear. If you picked 'It makes the sound louder at the source', remember that the sound is made at the phone, and the trumpet is at your ear.

flow.context: On day 2, you draw a bar chart and explain the result.

challenges.title: A Doorbell Without Sound: tell someone who cannot hear that a visitor has come
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a signal for the front door that works for a person who cannot hear it, and test it from another room.
challenges.problem: A visitor is at the front door. Someone in the kitchen cannot hear a bell. Design a signal that tells them a visitor is at the door, using light, movement or touch, with no sound.
constraints: The signal must work with no sound at all.
It must be noticed by a person in another room, at least 5 metres away, who is busy and not looking at the door.
Use only things you already have at home, such as a torch, string, a flag, a phone and cloth.
A helper wearing earmuffs tests it. The helper is not allowed to peek at the door.
materials: a battery torch that can be switched on and off (no mains lamp and no long electric wires)
string, cloth or a small flag
a phone, which can make a light flash or vibrate on the table
tape and scissors, used by a grown-up
earmuffs for the helper who tests
general: A light that flashes on and off in the kitchen when someone presses a switch at the door.
A string tied from the door handle to a cloth flag that waves in the kitchen when the door is knocked.
creative: A phone on a table that vibrates when called, with a ring of cups to make the vibration more visible. Test whether the helper notices the movement.
Three light signals, each made with a different colour of cloth, that mean different visitors, such as family, a friend or a delivery.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch two ideas. Pick the one you think is best. Build it, and test it with a helper in another room. Did they notice it? How fast? What would make it better?

setup.art: A child sketching two doorbell ideas on paper: a flashing lamp and a string with a flag.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch two ideas for a doorbell without sound.

setup.art: A string running from a front door handle along a hallway to a cloth flag in the kitchen, with the flag raised.
setup.caption: 2. Build your signal and run it from the door to the other room.

setup.art: A helper in the kitchen wearing earmuffs looking up at a waving flag while a child at the door knocks.
setup.caption: 3. Test it with a helper who cannot hear the door.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to think about how a Deaf person might notice a visitor. Ask for two sketches.
flow.say: Some people cannot hear a doorbell. How could they find out that a visitor has come, with no sound at all? Think of light, movement or touch. Sketch two ideas.
flow.kid: How could someone who cannot hear know a visitor came? Sketch two ideas.

ask.q: What sort of signal would be easiest to notice if you were busy cooking?
good: A flashing light, because it catches the corner of my eye.
A waving flag, because it moves.
A vibration on the table, because I can feel it.

flow.parent: Many Deaf families already use flashing lights, vibrating pagers or phone alerts. Ask your child to think before they build. Do not use sound in the final signal.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Doorbell Without Sound challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Choose the better idea. Build it. Make it work from the door to the kitchen. Test that it works while you stand next to it.
flow.say: Choose the idea you like best. Build it, and check that it works when you press the switch or pull the string.
flow.kid: Pick your best idea. Build it. Test it.
flow.parent: A grown-up should do any cutting or taping. Make sure strings run along walls where nobody will trip. Use only a battery torch or a phone light, never mains wiring or an extension cord laid across the floor.
flow.context: In this step, you build your signal and check that it works.

flow.do: Ask your helper to put on earmuffs, go to the kitchen and get busy with a task. Go to the door and use your signal. Time how long they take to notice. Ask them how it felt.
flow.say: Helper, put on the earmuffs and do something in the kitchen. I will go to the door and use my signal. I will time how long it takes you to notice. Don't look at the door.
flow.kid: The helper wears earmuffs and works in the kitchen. Use your signal. Time it.
flow.parent: The helper pretends to be someone who cannot hear. Be respectful. Real Deaf people have many ways of managing, and we are only testing an idea. Record the time and what the helper says.

check.q: Your signal was noticed in 3 seconds by the helper who was facing it, and in 20 seconds when the helper had their back to it. What does this tell you?
options: A signal that can be seen from any direction is better
The helper was not trying
Signals are not useful in kitchens
check.why: A person cannot notice a signal they are not facing. A light that fills the room or a vibration that can be felt works from any direction. If you chose 'The helper was not trying', remember that the test was the same each time and only the direction changed.

flow.context: In this step, you test your signal with a helper who cannot hear the door.

flow.do: Talk about what worked and what could be better. Change one thing and test again. Ask your child how they would improve it for a real home.
flow.say: What worked well? What did not? Change one thing and try again. How would you make the signal better for a real home?
flow.kid: What worked? What did not? Change one thing. Test again.
flow.think: Many Deaf people use flashing lights or vibrating alerts at home. What other things in a home use sound to tell us something, and how could each one be changed to use light or touch?
flow.parent: Good answers include: a smoke alarm, a pressure cooker whistle, a baby's cry, a phone ringing, a kettle, a car horn. Each can be matched with a light, a vibration or a visual signal.

items.p: A clap happens close to your right ear. Which ear gets the sound first, and which hears it a little louder?
opts: The right ear gets it first and hears it louder
The left ear gets it first and hears it louder
Both ears get it at the same time and equally loudly
items.why: The sound reaches the nearer ear first and is louder there, because the head blocks some sound from the far ear. The brain uses both clues.

items.p: A sound straight in front of you reaches both ears at the same ____.
items.why: Straight ahead is the same distance from both ears, so the sound arrives together and equally loud. That is why front and back are hard to tell apart.

items.p: Why is it harder to say where a sound is with one ear covered?
opts: The brain has no second ear to compare with
The sound becomes quieter in the air
The covered ear is the one that finds direction
items.why: Direction comes from comparing two ears. With one ear covered, the time and loudness differences are lost, so the brain must guess.

items.p: A whisper is about 30 decibels and a conversation is about 60 decibels, so the conversation has twice the sound energy of the whisper.
items.why: False. 30 decibels more is three steps of 10, and each step is 10 times the energy. So the conversation has 1,000 times the energy.

items.p: How many times more sound energy does a sound have if it is 10 decibels higher?
opts: 10 times
2 times
10 more units
items.why: Every 10 decibels is a multiplication by 10 in energy. That is why the numbers on the scale stay small even for huge differences.

items.p: At 85 decibels the safe listening time is about 8 hours, and each 3 decibels more halves it. About how long is it safe at 94 decibels?
opts: About 1 hour
About 4 hours
About 15 minutes
items.why: 94 is 9 more than 85, which is three steps of 3. Halve 8 hours three times: 4 hours, 2 hours, 1 hour.

items.p: Three of these are things the ear does with a sound. Which one is not?
opts: The ear flap collects sound and guides it in
Three tiny bones pass the sound on to the cochlea
Hair cells turn the wave into signals for the brain
The ear makes the sound louder at its source
items.why: The ear collects, passes on and detects sound. The source of a sound is outside the ear, and the ear cannot change it.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: You need these words to talk about hearing.
pairs: the ear flap on the side of the head
a loud sound hiding a quiet one
the coiled tube where hair cells turn waves into signals
the unit for how strong a sound is
hearing ringing when there is no sound outside

items.p: Is each one a clue the brain can use to find the direction of a sound, or not?
items.why: The brain uses the time, the loudness, the folds of the ear flap and the changes when the head turns. The temperature of the room and the colour of the walls do not help.
items: the sound reaches one ear before the other
the sound is louder in one ear
the sound changes when you turn your head

items.p: Put these in order along the cochlea, from where the wave peaks first (the narrow start) to where it peaks last (the far end).
items.why: High pitches make the wave peak near the start of the cochlea. Low pitches make it peak near the far end.

items.p: Hair cells destroyed by very loud noise grow back in a few weeks, so loud noise never causes lasting harm.
items.why: False. In people, hair cells do not grow back. Loud noise can cause lasting loss of hearing, often with no pain at the time.

items.p: You cannot hear a whisper while a tap runs hard. What is the best explanation?
opts: The whisper still reaches your ear, but the louder noise hides it
The whisper never leaves the speaker's mouth
Your ears stop working when there is noise
items.why: This is called masking. The louder sound moves the same part of the ear as the quiet one, so the quiet one is lost.

items.p: Label the model of the basilar membrane: the narrow stiff end, the wide soft end, where high pitches peak, and where low pitches peak.
items.why: The narrow, stiff end is the start, where high pitches peak. The wide, soft end is the far end, where low pitches peak.
items.art: A long strip, narrow at the left and wide at the right, with four blank label lines pointing to the left end, the right end, a place near the left end and a place near the right end.

items.p: Explain to a friend why covering one ear makes it harder to say where a sound is.
items.a: Two ears hear a sound a tiny bit differently. The nearer ear gets it first and louder. The brain compares them to work out the direction. With one ear covered, there is nothing to compare, so the brain has to guess.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two ears get slightly different sounds, that the brain compares them, and that one ear removes the comparison.

items.p: Draw a head seen from above with a clap on the right side. Draw a line from the clap to each ear, and show which line is shorter.
items.a: A head with two ears, a clap on the right, a short line to the right ear and a longer line to the left ear.
items.why: The clap is closer to the right ear, so the sound reaches it first and is a little louder there. The longer line shows that it takes more time to reach the left ear.
items.art: A blank circle for a head seen from above, with two small ears and a clap marked on the right.

items.p: In a noisy room, which of these helps a speaker be heard?
opts: Face the listener, come closer and speak clearly
Turn away from the listener and mumble
Speak as quickly as possible
items.why: Coming closer makes the voice louder than the noise. Facing the listener lets them see the lips, which helps the brain fill in what the ear misses. Speaking clearly helps too.

items.p: Sound travels about 340 metres each second. Your two ears are about 20 centimetres apart. About how much longer does a clap right beside one ear take to reach the other ear?
opts: About 0.0006 seconds
About 0.6 seconds
About 6 seconds
items.why: 0.2 metres divided by 340 metres each second is about 0.0006 seconds. This is too short to notice, but the brain can use it.

items.p: In open air a steady sound reads 60 decibels at 1 metre. About what will it read at 2 metres?
opts: About 54 decibels
About 30 decibels
About 120 decibels
items.why: In open air, each doubling of the distance takes off about 6 decibels. 60 take away 6 is 54. Halving the number to get 30 is a common slip.

items.p: Every ____ decibels more means 10 times as much sound energy.
items.why: The decibel scale is built so that each step of 10 multiplies the energy by 10.

items.p: At 85 decibels the safe time is about 8 hours, and every 3 decibels more halves it. About how long is it safe at 91 decibels?
opts: About 2 hours
About 4 hours
About 30 minutes
items.why: 91 is 6 more than 85, which is two steps of 3. Halve 8 hours twice: 4 hours, then 2 hours.

items.p: A sound that comes from exactly behind you is exactly the same distance from both ears.
items.why: True. Straight ahead and straight behind are both the same distance from each ear, so the time and loudness clues are the same. That is why head turns help.

items.p: Match each animal to where or how she or he hears.
items.why: Ears turn up in many places. In each, a thin skin or a hair is moved by sound.
pairs: ears on her front legs, below the knees
ears on the sides of her belly
ear stones inside her head, and sensors along her sides
ear openings at different heights on her head

items.p: Does each description fit a hearing aid, or a cochlear implant?
items.why: A hearing aid makes sound louder for hair cells that still work. A cochlear implant sends signals straight to the hearing nerve.
items: makes sound louder for hair cells that still work
sends signals straight to the hearing nerve
has a microphone, an amplifier and a tiny speaker
needs an operation to place wires inside the cochlea
sits in or behind the ear with no operation

items.p: Put these sounds in order from the quietest to the loudest.
a: a firecracker going off close by
items.why: They are about 20, 60, 95 and 140 decibels.
items: a firecracker going off close by

items.p: Three of these help a speaker be heard in a noisy place. Which does not?
opts: Come closer to the listener
Let the listener watch your mouth
Speak clearly and a little more slowly
Turn your back so the noise is behind you
items.why: Turning away hides your mouth and sends your voice the wrong way. The other three raise the voice above the noise or help the listener understand.

items.p: A thin high whistle is easier to follow over low drums than a low voice is. What is the best reason?
opts: Its pitch is far from the drums' pitch, so it is hidden less
It is always much louder than the drums
The drums cannot make any high sounds
items.why: Masking is strongest for sounds close in pitch to the noise. A sound far away in pitch is hidden less, and the ear is very sensitive to high pitches.

items.p: Which description of the basilar membrane is right?
opts: It is narrow and stiff at the start and wide and soft at the far end
It is wide and stiff at the start and narrow and soft at the far end
It is the same width and stiffness all along
items.why: This change in width and stiffness is why high pitches peak near the start and low pitches near the far end.

items.p: A friend says: 'A sound is only a sound if somebody hears it.' Do you agree? Give a reason.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side. One side says a sound is the wave in the air, and it is there with no one to hear. The other says loudness and pitch exist only in a listener, so without a listener there is only a wave.
items.why: Either answer is fine with a clear reason, and the best answers say what the other side gets right.

items.p: Explain why a steady fridge hum is harder to place than a short click.
items.a: A click starts at one moment, so one ear gets it a tiny bit before the other, and the brain can compare. A steady hum has no clear start, so it gives the brain much less to compare.
items.why: A strong answer says that a click has a clear start, so the difference in time between the ears is easy to use, and a steady hum does not.

items.p: A heavy branch falls to the ground in a forest, with nobody there to hear it. Two friends argue about whether it made a sound.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason from what you know about waves and hearing, and says what the other person has right.
items.why: Both have a point. The falling branch makes a wave in the air whether anyone is there. What we call loudness and pitch are what a listener makes of the wave.

views.says: Yes. The branch made a wave in the air. A sound is that wave, and it was there with nobody listening.
No. The wave is only squeezes in the air. A sound is what someone hears. With nobody there, there is only a wave.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about waves and hearing. Then say one thing the other person has right.

items.p: Label the head seen from above: sound source, nearer ear, farther ear, head shadow.
items.why: The sound reaches the nearer ear first. The head blocks some of it from the farther ear, and that blocked area is the head shadow.
items.art: A head seen from above with a speaker on the right, a shaded area behind the head on the left, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Draw an ear trumpet beside an ear, pointing at a sound source. Draw arrows to show sound waves entering the wide mouth.
items.a: A cone with a wide opening towards the sound, a narrow end near the ear, and arrows going in at the wide end and along to the narrow end.
items.why: A wide mouth collects more of the spreading sound and guides it to the small opening at the ear.
items.art: A blank space with a small ear drawn on the right and a speaker on the left.

items.p: A cochlear implant gives exactly the same sound as healthy hair cells would.
items.why: False. A cochlear implant works in a different way, with about twenty wires instead of thousands of hair cells. The sound is different, but many people learn to understand speech with it.

items.p: One sound is 20 decibels and another is 50 decibels. How many times more sound energy does the louder one have?
opts: 1,000 times
30 times
2.5 times
items.why: 50 is 30 more than 20, which is three steps of 10. 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000.

items.p: A drill is 100 decibels. A pair of earplugs lowers sound by about 20 decibels. About how long is it safe to listen with the earplugs in?
opts: Many hours, because 80 decibels is below 85
About 15 minutes
No time at all
items.why: 100 take away 20 is 80 decibels, which is below the 85 decibel limit for 8 hours. Without earplugs, the safe time at 100 would be only about 15 minutes.

items.p: A sound of 8,000 hertz and a sound of 1,000 hertz reach the cochlea. Which one makes the wave peak nearer the start?
opts: The 8,000 hertz sound
The 1,000 hertz sound
They peak in the same place
items.why: Higher pitches peak nearer the narrow, stiff start of the basilar membrane. Lower pitches peak further along.

items.p: A child has a cochlear implant. Which part of a healthy ear do the tiny wires take the place of?
opts: The hair cells
The ear flap
The eardrum
items.why: The wires send signals straight to the hearing nerve, taking the place of the hair cells that do not work.

items.p: Doctors check a baby's hearing by recording the faint sounds the baby's own ear gives out. These sounds are called ____ emissions.
items.why: Healthy outer hair cells push on the membrane, and the push is so strong that the ear itself gives out a faint sound. A damaged ear gives none.

items.p: A person who hears with only one ear can still get some idea of where a sound is by turning the head.
items.why: True. As the head turns, the sound gets louder or quieter in the working ear, and the brain uses the change. It is not as accurate as two ears, but it helps.

items.p: Match each situation to the idea it shows.
items.why: Each is a different thing the ear and brain do.
pairs: Not hearing a whisper while a tap runs hard
Following one friend's voice in a crowded hall
Hearing a ringing with no sound outside
Pointing to a click with your eyes shut
finding sound direction with two ears

items.p: Is each cause of hearing loss one that doctors can often treat, or one that damages hair cells?
items.why: A blocked ear can often be cleared, and fluid behind the eardrum can be treated. Hair cells damaged by noise or age do not grow back.
items: fluid behind the eardrum after a cold
years of very loud factory noise
hair cells worn out with age

items.p: Put these in order of how long it is safe to listen, from the shortest time to the longest.
a: a firecracker going off close by
items.why: A firecracker at about 140 decibels can hurt at once. A motorbike at about 95 decibels is safe for about 45 minutes. A mixer-grinder at about 85 is safe for about 8 hours. A whisper at about 30 is safe all day.
items: a firecracker going off close by

items.p: Three of these protect your hearing. Which one does not?
opts: Turning the headphones down
Moving away from a loud speaker
Wearing earplugs near fireworks
Pushing a cotton bud deep into the ear to clean it
items.why: Nothing should be pushed into the ear. A cotton bud can push wax deeper and can hurt the eardrum. The ear cleans itself.

items.p: A girl is lost in a crowd, and a relative blows a whistle. What is the best way to find the direction of the whistle?
opts: Turn her head until the whistle sounds the same in both ears, and then turn it a little to check front from back
Shut her ears and listen with her eyes
Run in the direction she feels like
items.why: When both ears hear the whistle equally, it is in front or behind. A small head turn tells which, because the sound moves to a different ear for each.

items.p: A newborn baby cannot say what she hears. How can doctors check her hearing with a tiny microphone placed in her ear?
items.a: A healthy cochlea gives out faint sounds of its own, made by the outer hair cells. A tiny microphone in the ear can record them, with no need for the baby to do anything. If the ear gives out the sound, the hair cells are working.
items.why: A strong answer says that a healthy ear makes faint sounds, that the microphone picks them up, and that the baby does not need to respond.

items.p: Many Deaf people say that a sign language is a real language. Give two reasons from what you know.
items.a: Sign languages have their own grammar and words, and they can say anything a spoken language can. Children learn them in the same stages as spoken languages, and they have jokes, stories and poems.
items.why: A strong answer gives two reasons, such as grammar, new words, jokes and poems, and the same stages of learning.

items.p: Two people sit in the same room. One hears with two working ears and the other with one. How might their experiences of the room differ?
items.a: The person with two ears can find where sounds are by comparing the two ears. The person with one ear has fewer clues, so places of sounds are harder to tell, and they may turn their head more. They also hear less well in noise, because it is harder to separate voices.
items.why: A strong answer says that two ears give direction clues, that one ear gives fewer, and that noise and crowds are harder.

items.p: A school plans a sports day with a loudspeaker at about 100 decibels for two hours.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, uses the safe time rule, and says what the other person has right.
items.why: Both views have a point. A sports day is exciting, and it is only one day. But at 100 decibels the safe time is about 15 minutes, and hair cells that are lost do not grow back.

views.says: It makes the day exciting, and it is only one day in the year. Nobody will be hurt.

views.who: A parent who is a doctor
views.says: At 100 decibels, the safe time is only about 15 minutes. Two hours can damage hair cells that never grow back.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason using the safe time rule. Then say one thing the other person has right.

items.p: Label the inner ear: cochlea, balance canals, ear stone patch, nerve to the brain.
items.why: The snail-shaped cochlea is for hearing. The three loops and the stone patches are for balance. The nerve carries the signals to the brain.
items.art: An inner ear with a coiled cochlea, three loops at right angles, a small patch with stones and a nerve leaving, with four blank label lines.

quiz.p: A clap happens on your left. Which ear hears it first?
opts: The left ear
The right ear
Both together
quiz.why: The sound reaches the nearer ear first, and a little louder.

quiz.p: A girl points well to clicks with two ears and badly with one ear covered. What does this show?
opts: The brain finds direction by comparing the two ears
The covered ear is the only one that finds direction
Clicks are quieter when one ear is covered
quiz.why: Direction is worked out by comparing what the two ears hear. With one ear covered, the comparison is lost.

quiz.p: A sound of 90 decibels has 10 times the energy of a sound of 80 decibels.
quiz.why: True. Each 10 decibels is a multiplication by 10 in energy.

quiz.p: A sound is 100 decibels. What is the safest choice?
opts: Move away or use earplugs
Listen for 3 hours
Stand closer to hear it better
quiz.why: At 100 decibels, the safe time is only about 15 minutes. Moving away or using earplugs lowers the level a lot.

quiz.p: You cannot hear your friend over a loud fan. Which is most likely to help?
opts: Come closer and face each other
Turn your backs to each other
Speak in a whisper
quiz.why: Being closer makes the voice louder than the noise, and seeing the lips helps the brain understand.

quiz.p: Where does the wave on the basilar membrane peak for a very low sound?
opts: Near the wide, soft far end
Near the narrow, stiff start
It peaks everywhere at once
quiz.why: Low pitches make the wave peak far along the membrane, where it is wide and soft. High pitches peak near the start.

quiz.p: How does a cochlear implant help a person to hear?
opts: It sends signals from a microphone straight to the hearing nerve
It makes the sound louder in the ear canal
It replaces the eardrum with a drum
quiz.why: The tiny wires in the cochlea excite the hearing nerve directly, without needing working hair cells.

quiz.p: Sign languages are real languages with their own grammar.
quiz.why: True. Linguists have shown this since the 1960s. They can say anything a spoken language can.

quiz.p: Which animal hears with feathery antennae?
opts: A male mosquito
A cricket
A barn owl
quiz.why: A male mosquito follows the wingbeat of a female with his antennae. A cricket hears with her front legs, and an owl hears with ears on her head.

quiz.p: Why is a thin steady whistle easier to follow among loud drums than a low voice?
opts: Its pitch is far from the drums, so it is hidden less
It is always louder than a drum
Drums cannot make any sound in a crowd
quiz.why: Masking is strongest for sounds that are close in pitch to the noise. A sound that is far from it in pitch is hidden less.

quiz.p: At 85 decibels the safe time is about 8 hours, and every 3 decibels more halves it. About how long is it safe at 97 decibels?
opts: About 30 minutes
About 2 hours
About 4 hours
quiz.why: 97 is 12 more than 85, which is four steps of 3. Halve 8 hours four times: 4 hours, 2 hours, 1 hour, 30 minutes.

quiz.p: A bat's squeak is too high for people to hear. A moth hears it and dives. What does this suggest about sounds?
opts: Different animals hear different ranges of sound
Bats' squeaks are not real sounds
Moths hear better than all other animals
quiz.why: The wave is in the air for every animal, but each animal's ears pick up only some pitches. People's ears cannot pick up a bat's squeak.

applications: Hearing aids make sounds louder for people whose hair cells still work but have become less sensitive, for example in old age.
Cochlear implants let many children who were born deaf learn to understand speech.
Hospitals check newborn babies' hearing in a minute or two by recording the faint sounds the ear gives out, so that help can begin early.
Earplugs and ear defenders protect the hair cells of people who work near drills, machines and aircraft.
Noise rules set safe limits for homes, schools, hospitals and firecrackers, and sound meters are used to check them.
Concert halls and classrooms are designed so that sound reaches every seat clearly, and so that echoes and noise do not hide speech.
Music files such as MP3s are made smaller by dropping sounds that a louder sound next to them would hide anyway, which uses the idea of masking.
Stereo sound and surround sound use the time and loudness differences between two ears to make a sound seem to come from a place.
Sign language interpreters and captions allow Deaf people to follow lessons, news and films in India.
Ear trumpets, megaphones and hearing horns use a wide mouth and a narrow end to gather and focus sound.

open_questions.q: How does the brain join the clues from two ears, the shape of the ear flap, head turns and the eyes into one place in space?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know each clue and can measure how well people use them. They do not yet know how the brain combines all of them so quickly and so well.

open_questions.q: Can people's damaged hair cells ever be made to grow back?
open_questions.why_open: Birds and fish can grow new hair cells after damage, but people cannot. Scientists are testing ways to make human ears do the same, but there is no sure cure yet.

open_questions.q: What really causes the ringing of tinnitus?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think it starts in the damaged ear, and others think the brain makes it. It probably involves both, but nobody can yet explain it fully or cure it.

open_questions.q: How do people with a cochlear implant experience music?
open_questions.why_open: Many understand speech well, but find music flat. Scientists are studying how to give implants a richer sound, and what music is like for each person.

open_questions.q: Why does music, which does nothing for food or safety, move us so strongly?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have many ideas, from group bonding to the way the brain predicts patterns, but nobody knows which are right, and the answer may be a mixture.

open_questions.q: Is a sound a wave in the air, or what a listener hears?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists and philosophers use the word in different ways. The wave is certain. Whether the sound is the wave or the hearing is a question about the meaning of the word, and people still argue about it.

maths.problem: Sound travels about 340 metres each second. How far does it travel in one hundredth of a second, which is 0.01 seconds? Your two ears are about 20 centimetres apart. Is that more or less than the distance sound travels in one thousandth of a second?
maths.answer: 3.4 metres in one hundredth of a second. In one thousandth it is 34 centimetres, so 20 centimetres takes less than a thousandth, about 6 ten-thousandths of a second.
maths.explain: 340 divided by 100 is 3.4 metres. 340 divided by 1,000 is 0.34 metres, which is 34 centimetres. Your ears are 20 centimetres apart, which is less than 34, so a sound crosses between them in less than a thousandth of a second.
maths.context: In the Sound Clock, the brain compares the moments a sound reaches each of your two ears, which are about 20 centimetres apart.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a speed by 100 or 1,000 shows how short the time between your ears really is, and why the brain's skill is so remarkable.

maths.problem: A whisper is about 25 decibels. A mixer-grinder is about 85 decibels. The difference is 60 decibels. How many tens is that, and how many times as much energy does the mixer-grinder have?
maths.answer: 6 tens. The mixer-grinder has 1,000,000 times as much energy.
maths.explain: 60 divided by 10 is 6 steps of 10. Each step multiplies the energy by 10. So 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000,000. That is one million.
maths.context: In the Decibel Ladder, every 10 decibels more means 10 times the sound energy.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying 10 again and again shows how a small change in decibels is a huge change in energy.

maths.problem: At 85 decibels the safe time is about 8 hours, and every 3 decibels more halves it. Fill in the safe time at 88, 91, 94, 97 and 100 decibels, and say what pattern you see.
maths.answer: 4 hours, 2 hours, 1 hour, 30 minutes and 15 minutes. Each time, the number is half the one before.
maths.explain: 88 is 3 more than 85, so halve 8 hours to get 4 hours. Halve again for 91, to get 2 hours. Then 1 hour, then 30 minutes, then 15 minutes. The pattern is halving.
maths.context: In the Decibel Ladder, the safe time for a loud sound shrinks as the decibel number goes up.
maths.why_maths: A halving pattern lets you work out safe times for sounds you have not been told about.

maths.problem: In the Sound Clock, a child got 13 of 16 clicks exactly right with two ears and 6 of 16 exactly right with one ear covered. Which round was more than half right? How many fewer did the child get right with one ear covered?
maths.answer: The two-ear round was more than half right. The child got 7 fewer right with one ear covered.
maths.explain: Half of 16 is 8. 13 is more than 8, and 6 is less than 8. The difference is 13 take away 6, which is 7.
maths.context: In the Sound Clock, you point to 16 clicks with two ears and then with one ear covered.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a score with half of the total tells you at once whether a round went well or badly.

maths.problem: A fan reads 60 decibels at 1 metre. In open air, every time you double the distance, the level drops by about 6 decibels. What would it read at 2 metres, 4 metres and 8 metres?
maths.explain: Doubling from 1 to 2 metres takes off 6, so 54. Doubling to 4 metres takes off 6 more, so 48. Doubling to 8 metres takes off 6 more, so 42.
maths.context: In Doubling the Distance, you measure how the sound level of a fan falls as you move away.
maths.why_maths: A subtracting pattern lets you predict the sound level at a distance you have not measured.

maths.problem: The unrolled cochlea is about 35 millimetres long. Our Paper Snail is 10 times as long. How long is the snail in millimetres and in centimetres? The real narrow end is 0.1 millimetres wide, and the wide end is five times wider. How wide is the wide end?
maths.answer: 350 millimetres, which is 35 centimetres. The wide end is 0.5 millimetres.
maths.explain: 35 times 10 is 350 millimetres. There are 10 millimetres in a centimetre, so that is 35 centimetres. Five times 0.1 millimetres is 0.5 millimetres.
maths.context: In the Paper Snail, you make a model of the cochlea that is 10 times its real length.
maths.why_maths: Scaling and changing units lets you build a big model of something too small to see.

maths.problem: Each ear has about 15,000 hair cells. How many hair cells are there in two ears? A very loud night destroys one in ten of them in each ear. How many are lost in all?
maths.answer: 30,000 hair cells in two ears, and 3,000 lost in all.
maths.explain: 15,000 plus 15,000 is 30,000. One in ten of 15,000 is 1,500 in each ear. 1,500 plus 1,500 is 3,000 lost in all. They do not grow back.
maths.context: The card 'The cochlea sorts high and low pitches along its length' says each ear has about 15,000 hair cells. Loud noise can destroy them for good.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of a large number shows how much hearing could be lost in one loud night.

maths.problem: A hearing test uses pitches that double each time: 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000 hertz. How many times is the pitch doubled between 250 and 8,000? How many times higher is 8,000 than 250?
maths.explain: 250 to 500 is one doubling, then 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000. That is five doublings. 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 is 32. So 8,000 is 32 times 250.
maths.context: An audiogram checks a person's hearing at pitches that double each time.
maths.why_maths: Repeated doubling shows how far apart the pitches on an audiogram really are.

maths.problem: In Hiding a Whisper, a girl got 5, 5, 5, 4 and 2 digits right at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 metres in a quiet room, and 5, 5, 3, 1 and 0 with the tap running gently. How far did the whisper reach in each case, if reach means the furthest distance with 4 or 5 right? How much shorter was the reach with the tap?
maths.answer: 4 metres in quiet and 2 metres with the tap. The reach was 2 metres shorter, half as far.
maths.explain: In quiet, 4 right at 4 metres, so the reach is 4 metres. With the tap, 5 right at 2 metres but only 3 at 3 metres, so the reach is 2 metres. 4 take away 2 is 2 metres, which is half.
maths.context: In Hiding a Whisper, you whisper five digits at each of five distances, and score the digits right.
maths.why_maths: Reading a table carefully and comparing two numbers shows how much a noise cuts the reach of a whisper.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Sound Clock is the main test: a chair, a katori and spoon, eight paper slips and a soft ear cover. The parent moves silently to each place and clicks once, so the results depend on a steady hand and soft socks. The expected scores, about 11 of 16 with two ears, about 5 with one ear covered and about 14 with head turns, are estimates, and a family may see different numbers. The steps say nothing goes inside the ear. Hiding a Whisper needs a clear space of 6 metres and a tap or fan. A flat without a long corridor can use a shorter row with 0.5 metre steps. The scores of whisper reach are estimates too. Doubling the Distance needs a phone with a free sound meter app, and phone microphones are rough, so the unit says to look at the pattern, not the exact numbers. The Paper Snail marks come from the usual map of pitch along the cochlea, rounded. Feel the Music works best with a clear drum beat at conversation volume. Facts to check before use: the 2000 Indian noise rules (55 decibels by day and 45 by night in residential areas, and about 125 decibels at 4 metres for firecrackers), the safe-time table (the NIOSH rule of 85 decibels for 8 hours and 3 decibels per halving), the decibel values on the Decibel Ladder cards (rounded, and some, such as the wedding loudspeaker, vary a lot), and the hair cell numbers (about 15,000 in each ear).
